definition: The speed at which something changes or progresses.
example: The population grew at a rate of two per cent a year.
distinctions: A growth rate describes change relative to time or a starting amount; population size describes how many people there are.

originalSense.definition: The relative speed of change or progress.
originalSense.example: The rate of production at the factory is skyrocketing.

distinctionTask.prompt: The graph shows the annual _____ of population growth.
distinctionTask.explanation: Rate describes the speed of growth; total describes the whole amount.

definition: The price charged for a particular item or service.
example: Ask the hotel for its rate for a single room.
distinctions: A rate often states a price for a unit or category of service; a bill states the amount actually owed.

originalSense.definition: The price of (an individual) thing; cost.
originalSense.example: He asked quite a rate to take me to the airport.

definition: A fixed price or charge for a particular class of goods or services.
example: The hotel offers a reduced rate for students.
distinctions: A flat rate is fixed for the stated service; a variable charge changes with usage or other conditions.

originalSense.definition: A set price or charge for all examples of a given case, commodity, service etc.
originalSense.example: Postal rates here are low.

definition: An amount of pay calculated for a unit of working time.
example: The hourly rate rises after the probation period.
distinctions: An hourly rate states pay per hour; a salary is usually expressed as a yearly amount.

originalSense.definition: A wage calculated in relation to a unit of time.
originalSense.example: We pay an hourly rate of between $10 – $15 per hour depending on qualifications and experience.

distinctionTask.prompt: The job pays an hourly _____ of fifteen pounds.
distinctionTask.explanation: An hourly rate is pay per hour; a salary is usually quoted for a year.

definition: A tax, especially one charged by a local authority on property.
example: The shop owner pays business rates to the local council.
distinctions: Rates are a form of local taxation; rent is payment to a property owner.
usage: Often plural. The exact tax system depends on the country or region.

originalSense.definition: Any of various taxes, especially those levied by a local authority.
originalSense.example: I hardly have enough left every month to pay the rates.

definition: To assign someone or something a rank or level.
example: The hotel is rated four stars.
distinctions: Rate assigns a level; rank usually places items in an order relative to one another.

originalSense.definition: To assign or be assigned a particular rank or level.
originalSense.example: She is rated fourth in the country.

definition: To judge the quality or value of something.
example: Please rate the service on a scale from one to five.
distinctions: Rate makes an evaluation; estimate often gives an approximate quantity or cost.

originalSense.definition: To evaluate or estimate the value of.
originalSense.example: They rate his talents highly.

definition: To consider someone or something to have a particular quality.
example: The panel rates her as a strong candidate.
distinctions: Rate someone as states an assessment; regard someone as can express a broader opinion without a scale.

originalSense.definition: To consider or regard.
originalSense.example: He rated this book brilliant.

definition: To deserve a particular response, level of attention or treatment.
example: The discovery rates a mention in the annual report.
distinctions: Rate in this use means deserve; rate a service means evaluate it.

originalSense.definition: To deserve; to be worth.
originalSense.example: The view here hardly rates a mention in the travel guide.

definition: To specify the safe operating limits of a machine or electrical device.
example: The cable is rated for a maximum current of ten amperes.
distinctions: A device's rating states a specified operating limit; its actual consumption depends on how it is used.

originalSense.definition: To determine the limits of safe functioning for a machine or electrical device.
originalSense.example: The transformer is rated at 10 watts.

definition: To think highly of someone or something.
example: I really rate her work as a translator.
distinctions: Rate in this informal use means admire or think well of; rate something on a scale is a neutral evaluation.
usage: Informal; especially British English.

originalSense.definition: To like; to think highly of.
originalSense.example: The customers don't rate the new burgers.

definition: Money or wealth available to start a business or produce goods and services.
example: The founders raised enough capital to open a small factory.
distinctions: Capital provides resources for a business; profit is what remains from revenue after costs.

originalSense.definition: Money and wealth: the means to acquire or produce goods and services, especially in a non-barter system.
originalSense.example: Near-synonym: assets

distinctionTask.prompt: Before it could start trading, the company needed to raise _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Capital finances the business; profit is what remains after costs once it trades.

definition: Produced assets, such as machinery and buildings, used to make goods or provide services.
example: The investment increased the factory's stock of physical capital.
distinctions: Physical capital consists of productive assets; financial capital refers to funds available to finance activity.

originalSense.definition: Already-produced durable goods available for use as a factor of production, such as tools and bulldozers (equipment) and office buildings (structures).
originalSense.example: Near-synonym: assets

definition: Investors and owners of wealth considered as a group.
example: The article examines the relationship between capital and labour.
distinctions: Capital here refers collectively to owners or investors; it does not name a city or a single sum of money.

originalSense.definition: The capitalist class; investors considered collectively with respect to their societal (economic, political, cultural, etc.) influence.
originalSense.example: The markets crashing symbolized capital’s discontent with the tax reforms passed.

definition: A city that serves as a seat of government for a country or region.
example: Canberra is the capital of Australia.
distinctions: A capital is a seat of government; a country's largest city may be somewhere else.

originalSense.definition: A city designated as a legislative seat by the government or some other authority, often the city in which the government is located; otherwise the most important city within a country or a subdivision of it.
originalSense.example: Washington D.C. is the capital of the United States of America.

distinctionTask.prompt: Canberra is the _____ of Australia.
distinctionTask.explanation: Capital names the governmental city; capitol refers to a legislative building in some countries.

definition: A city regarded as an important centre for a particular activity.
example: The city has become a regional capital of design.
distinctions: A fashion capital is an important centre of fashion; it need not be a seat of government.

originalSense.definition: The most important city in the field specified.
originalSense.example: Hollywood is the film capital, New York the theater capital, Las Vegas the gambling capital.

definition: An uppercase letter.
example: Write your name in capitals.
distinctions: A capital is an uppercase letter such as A; a lowercase letter is a.

originalSense.definition: An uppercase letter.

definition: Of the greatest importance.
example: Access to clean water is a matter of capital importance.
distinctions: Capital means crucial in this formal use; main is more usual in everyday descriptions of importance.
usage: Formal; usually in phrases such as of capital importance.

originalSense.definition: Of prime importance.
originalSense.example: a capital article in religion

definition: Serving as a seat of government.
example: The parliament is located in the capital city.
distinctions: Capital city identifies a governmental role; largest city identifies size.

originalSense.definition: Chief (in a political sense, as being the seat of the general government of a state or nation).
originalSense.example: London and Paris are capital cities.

definition: Involving or punishable by the death penalty.
example: The law classifies the offence as a capital crime.
distinctions: A capital offence may carry the death penalty; a serious offence does not necessarily do so.

originalSense.definition: Punishable by, or involving punishment by, death.
originalSense.example: capital punishment; capital murder

definition: Written in uppercase form.
example: Begin each sentence with a capital letter.
distinctions: Capital describes uppercase letters; capitol is a noun for a legislative building in some countries.

originalSense.definition: Uppercase.
originalSense.example: One begins a sentence with a capital letter.

distinctionTask.prompt: Begin the sentence with a _____ letter.
distinctionTask.explanation: Capital is the adjective for an uppercase letter; capitol names a building.

definition: The top part of a column, supporting the structure above it.
example: The stone capital is decorated with carved leaves.
distinctions: A capital is the top of an architectural column; the base is at the bottom.
usage: Architecture.

originalSense.definition: The uppermost part of a column.
originalSense.example: But a great wonder of this chamber, and a marvel to behold, was how the capital of every one of the four-and-twenty pillars was hewn from a single precious stone, carved by the hand of some sculptor of long ago into the living form of a monster: […]

definition: A local office of a financial institution.
example: The bank on the high street closes at four.
distinctions: Bank here means a branch or its premises; the institution may operate many branches.

originalSense.definition: A branch office of such an institution.

definition: A place or collection used to store important material for later use.
example: The hospital keeps donated blood in a blood bank.
distinctions: A blood bank stores blood; a financial bank holds money and provides financial services.

originalSense.definition: A safe and guaranteed place of storage for and retrieval of important items or goods.
originalSense.example: blood bank; data bank; sperm bank

definition: A small container used to save coins or money.
example: The child put a coin in her piggy bank.
distinctions: A piggy bank is a container for savings; a bank account is held by a financial institution.

originalSense.definition: A device used to store coins or currency.
originalSense.example: If you want to buy a bicycle, you need to put the money in your piggy bank.

definition: To use a bank for financial services.
example: Our business banks with a local credit union.
distinctions: Bank with names the institution you use; bank money means deposit it.

originalSense.definition: To deal with a bank or financial institution, or for an institution to provide financial services to a client.
originalSense.example: He banked with Barclays.

definition: To put money into a bank account.
example: Please bank the cheque before Friday.
distinctions: Bank a cheque means deposit it; cash a cheque means exchange it for cash.

originalSense.definition: To put into a bank (financial institution).
originalSense.example: I’m going to bank the money.

distinctionTask.prompt: Please _____ the cheque by depositing it in your account.
distinctionTask.explanation: Bank a cheque means deposit it; cash it means receive cash for it.

definition: To store something in a collection or facility for future use.
example: The researchers banked the seeds for future conservation work.
distinctions: Bank means store for future use here; it does not imply a financial transaction.

originalSense.definition: To store in a bank (storage).
originalSense.example: the procurement, banking or transplantation of cadaveric organs, eyes, or tissue

definition: The land along the edge of a river, lake or other watercourse.
example: We sat on the bank of the river and watched the boats.
distinctions: A bank borders a river or watercourse; shore is more usual for the edge of a sea or large lake.

originalSense.definition: An edge of river, lake, or other watercourse.
originalSense.example: Tiber trembled underneath her banks.

distinctionTask.prompt: They walked along the _____ of the narrow river.
distinctionTask.explanation: Bank is the usual word for land along a river; shore is more usual beside a sea or large lake.

definition: A shallow raised area of sand, mud or gravel under water.
example: The boat ran aground on a sand bank near the harbour.
distinctions: An underwater bank is a raised area beneath the surface; a river bank is land along a watercourse.

originalSense.definition: An elevation under the sea; a shallow area of shifting sand, gravel, mud, and so forth
originalSense.example: the banks of Newfoundland

definition: A raised slope or mound of earth, sand or similar material.
example: A grassy bank separates the road from the footpath.
distinctions: A bank can be a raised slope of land without bordering a river; an embankment is usually built for support or protection.

originalSense.definition: A slope of earth, sand, etc.; an embankment.

definition: The sideways tilt of an aircraft, especially while it turns.
example: The aircraft entered a gentle bank to the left.
distinctions: Bank is an aircraft's sideways tilt; pitch is its nose-up or nose-down angle.
usage: Aviation.

originalSense.definition: The incline of an aircraft, especially during a turn.

definition: To tilt sideways, especially while turning in flight.
example: The aircraft banked to the left as it approached the airport.
distinctions: An aircraft banks when it tilts sideways; it climbs when it gains height.

originalSense.definition: To roll or incline laterally in order to turn.

definition: A large mass of clouds.
example: A bank of dark clouds gathered over the hills.
distinctions: A bank of clouds describes their mass or grouping; a river bank describes a land edge.

originalSense.definition: A mass of clouds.
originalSense.example: The bank of clouds on the horizon announced the arrival of the predicted storm front.

definition: A row or group of similar objects arranged together.
example: The operator sat in front of a bank of monitors.
distinctions: A bank groups similar items together; a single monitor is not a bank.

originalSense.definition: A row or panel of items stored or grouped together.
originalSense.example: a bank of switches

definition: An amount of money that must be paid for a service.
example: There is no extra charge for delivery.
distinctions: A charge is an amount payable; a fine is a payment imposed as a penalty.

originalSense.definition: The amount of money levied for a service.
originalSense.example: There will be a charge of five dollars.

distinctionTask.prompt: There is an extra _____ of five pounds for delivery.
distinctionTask.explanation: A charge here is a service fee; a conviction is a court finding of guilt.

definition: An attack in which people rush towards an enemy.
example: The cavalry launched a charge across the open field.
distinctions: A charge is a rushing attack; a siege involves surrounding and attempting to capture a place over time.

originalSense.definition: An attack in which combatants rush towards an enemy in an attempt to engage in close combat.
originalSense.example: Pickett's Charge; the Charge of the Light Brigade

definition: A sudden, forceful movement forwards.
example: The runner made a final charge towards the finish line.
distinctions: This charge is a forceful movement; a financial charge is a fee.

originalSense.definition: A forceful forward movement.
originalSense.example: Abou Diaby should have added Arsenal's fourth in the 50th minute after he danced round a host of defenders on a charge towards goal

definition: A statement accusing someone of wrongdoing or a crime.
example: He denied the charge of theft.
distinctions: A charge is an accusation; a conviction means a court has found someone guilty.

originalSense.definition: An accusation.
originalSense.example: two charges of manslaughter

definition: An electrical property of matter that can be positive or negative.
example: An electron has a negative electric charge.
distinctions: Charge is measured in coulombs; current is the rate at which charge flows.

originalSense.definition: An electric charge.

distinctionTask.prompt: An electron carries a negative electric _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Charge is an electrical property of a particle; current is charge flowing per unit of time.

definition: Responsibility for supervising or looking after someone or something.
example: She took charge of the project when the manager left.
distinctions: In charge of means responsible for; in the charge of identifies the person who has that responsibility.

originalSense.definition: The scope of someone's responsibility.
originalSense.example: The child was in the nanny's charge.

definition: A person or thing entrusted to someone's care.
example: The teacher counted her young charges before the trip.
distinctions: A charge is the person being cared for; the person responsible is the carer or supervisor.
usage: Often plural; this use can sound formal or literary.

originalSense.definition: Someone or something entrusted to one's care, such as a child to a babysitter or a student to a teacher.
originalSense.example: The child was a charge of the nanny.

definition: To give someone a duty or responsibility.
example: The committee was charged with reviewing the safety procedures.
distinctions: Charged with reviewing assigns a duty; charged with theft makes a criminal accusation.
usage: Use charge someone with + a noun or an -ing form.

originalSense.definition: To assign a duty or responsibility to; to order.
originalSense.example: Moses […] charged you to love the Lord your God.

definition: To record an amount as owed by a particular account or person.
example: The hotel charged the meal to my room.
distinctions: Charge an amount to an account records who owes it; pay an amount settles a debt.

originalSense.definition: To assign (a debit) to an account.
originalSense.example: Let's charge this to marketing.

definition: To ask someone to pay a price for goods or services.
example: The museum charges ten pounds for admission.
distinctions: Charge is what a seller asks someone to pay; cost describes the price from the buyer's perspective.

originalSense.definition: To require payment (of) (a price or fee, for goods, services, etc.).
originalSense.example: to charge high for goods

definition: To pay for something using credit or an account.
example: I charged the tickets to my credit card.
distinctions: Charge a purchase uses credit or an account; pay cash transfers money immediately.

originalSense.definition: To pay on account, as by using a credit card.
originalSense.example: Can I charge my purchase to my credit card?

definition: To formally accuse someone of a crime.
example: Police charged the driver with dangerous driving.
distinctions: Charge someone with a crime makes an accusation; convict someone of a crime records a finding of guilt.

originalSense.definition: To formally accuse (a person) of a crime.
originalSense.example: I'm charging you with assault and battery.

distinctionTask.prompt: Police may _____ a suspect with theft before the case goes to court.
distinctionTask.explanation: Police charge someone with an offence; a court may later convict them of it.

definition: To move forwards quickly and forcefully.
example: The bull charged towards the fence.
distinctions: Charge suggests forceful forward movement; rush is a broader word for moving quickly.

originalSense.definition: To move forward quickly and forcefully, particularly in combat and/or on horseback.
originalSense.example: Faced with an enemy whose largest gun turrets weigh more than the entire ship, Johnston decides that running is boring, and instead pulls a full 180-degree turn and charges straight back at the attacking forces.

definition: A record or statement of financial transactions, including money received and spent.
example: The charity publishes its accounts at the end of each financial year.
distinctions: Accounts record financial activity; a bank account is an arrangement for holding money.
usage: Often plural when referring to an organisation’s financial records.

originalSense.definition: A registry of pecuniary transactions; a written or printed statement of business dealings or debts and credits, and also of other things subjected to a reckoning or review.
originalSense.example: The firm failed to file its accounts on time.

definition: An arrangement with a bank for holding money and recording deposits and withdrawals.
example: She transferred the rent from her savings account.
distinctions: An account holds or records your money; a balance is the amount in it.

originalSense.definition: A bank account.
originalSense.example: The money was refunded to her account.

definition: An explanation of why something happens or happened.
example: The report offers a convincing account of why the bridge failed.
distinctions: An explanatory account gives reasons or causes; a narrative account describes events.

originalSense.definition: A statement in general of reasons, causes, grounds, etc., explanatory of some event; a reason of an action to be done.
originalSense.example: Becoming more aware of the progress that scientists have made on behavioral fronts can reduce the risk that other natural scientists will resort to mystical agential accounts when they exceed the limits of their own disciplinary training.

definition: A reason for doing something, or the person for whose sake it is done.
example: Please do not change your plans on my account.
distinctions: On my account means for my sake; on account of the rain means because of the rain.
usage: Usually in phrases such as on someone’s account or on account of something.

originalSense.definition: A reason, grounds, consideration, motive; a person's sake.
originalSense.example: Don't trouble yourself on my account.

definition: A spoken or written description of events or experiences.
example: The witness gave a detailed account of the accident.
distinctions: An account describes events; an explanation focuses on why they happened.

originalSense.definition: A record of events; a relation or narrative.
originalSense.example: An account of a battle.

distinctionTask.prompt: The witness gave a detailed _____ of what happened.
distinctionTask.explanation: An account describes events; a balance is an amount remaining in an account.

definition: A judgement or estimation of someone or something.
example: The writer stands high in the critic’s account.
distinctions: Account here means someone’s estimation; opinion is more usual in modern everyday English.
usage: Rare or literary. The listed phrases illustrate this older use of account.

originalSense.definition: An estimate or estimation; valuation; judgment.
originalSense.example: To stand high in your account

definition: Importance, worth or esteem.
example: He dismissed the objections as being of little account.
distinctions: Of little account means of little importance; a small bank account refers to an amount of money.
usage: Formal or literary; often in of little account or of no account.

originalSense.definition: Importance; worth; value; esteem; judgement.
originalSense.example: There is a peculiarity in Homers manner of apoſtrophizing Eumæus, and ſpeaking of him in the ſecond perſon; it is generally apply'd by that Poet only to men of account' and diſtinction, and by it the Poet, as it were, addreſſes them with reſpect; […]

definition: A registered identity that allows someone to use a website, application or computer system.
example: Create an account before you save your progress.
distinctions: An account identifies a registered user; a password is one way to authenticate that user.

originalSense.definition: Authorization as a specific registered user in accessing a system.
originalSense.example: Since the system outage, I've been unable to log in to my account.

definition: A reckoning or calculation, or a record of that calculation.
example: The clerk kept an account of the number of sacks delivered.
distinctions: Account here is a reckoning; amount names the quantity being reckoned.
usage: Archaic in this general calculation sense. Count or calculation is usually clearer in modern writing.

originalSense.definition: A reckoning; computation; calculation; enumeration; a record of some reckoning.
originalSense.example: It seems that this severity weakened his frame, for three years syne come Martinmas he was taken ill with a fever of the bowels, and after a week's sickness he went to his account, where I trust he is accepted.

definition: Use, benefit or advantage gained from something.
example: She turned her experience abroad to good account in her new job.
distinctions: Turn experience to good account means use it beneficially; give an account means describe something.
usage: Usually in the expression turn or put something to good account.

originalSense.definition: Profit; advantage.
originalSense.example: The young man soon turned his woodworking skills to some account.

definition: To provide an explanation.
example: In obsolete usage, account could mean to provide an explanation.
distinctions: Modern English normally uses explain, or account for followed by the thing explained.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the historical meaning; it is not a source quotation or a model for modern writing.

originalSense.definition: To provide explanation.

definition: To count or reckon a quantity.
example: In the old chronology, years were accounted from the king’s accession.
distinctions: This older use means count; the modern phrase account for can mean explain or constitute.
usage: Archaic. Use count or reckon for this meaning in modern writing.

originalSense.definition: To count.
originalSense.example: neither the motion of the Moon, whereby moneths are computed; nor of the Sun, whereby years are accounted, consisteth of whole numbers, but admits of fractions, and broken parts, as we have already declared concerning the Moon.

definition: Used with a preposition in expressions such as account for, meaning explain or constitute, and account to, meaning report to someone.
example: Transport accounts for a third of the city’s emissions.
distinctions: Account for can explain a cause or state a proportion; account to identifies the person owed a report.
usage: Learn the whole expression. Account for and account to have different meanings and grammatical patterns.

originalSense.definition: Used in phrasal verbs: account for, account of, account to.

distinctionTask.prompt: Transport _____ for a third of the city’s emissions.
distinctionTask.explanation: Account for states a proportion here; count means enumerate.

definition: The condition of someone or something at a particular time.
example: The survey assessed the state of the local roads.
distinctions: State describes a condition; status often describes an official position or stage in a process.

originalSense.definition: A condition; a set of circumstances applying at any given time.
originalSense.example: a state of being

distinctionTask.prompt: The engineer inspected the building’s _____ of repair.
distinctionTask.explanation: State of repair describes the building’s condition; a statement is something said or written.

definition: High rank or the ceremony and grandeur associated with it.
example: The monarch travelled in state to the opening ceremony.
distinctions: In state describes ceremonial dignity; in a state usually describes a condition, often distress.
usage: Formal; especially in ceremonial expressions such as in state and lie in state.

originalSense.definition: High social standing or circumstance.
originalSense.example: in state

definition: A politically organised community or polity.
example: The historian compared the institutions of several ancient states.
distinctions: A state is a political community; a nation can describe people sharing a history or identity.

originalSense.definition: A polity or community.
originalSense.example: Never do anything against conscience even if the state demands it.

definition: A possible value or configuration of a stochastic process.
example: The model has two states: working and failed.
distinctions: A state is a possible condition in the model; a transition is a change from one state to another.
usage: Probability and stochastic modelling.

originalSense.definition: An element of the range of the random variables that define a random process.

definition: A type of situation expressed by a verb or predicate that describes a condition rather than a changing event.
example: Knowing the answer is a state, while discovering it is an event.
distinctions: Know describes a state; discover describes an event that brings about a change.
usage: Linguistics: lexical aspect. A state is not restricted to the present tense.

originalSense.definition: The lexical aspect (aktionsart) of verbs or predicates that do not change over time.
originalSense.example: […]distinctions among states of affairs are reflected to a striking degree in distinctions among Aktionsart types. That is, situations are expressed by state verbs or predicates, events by achievement verbs or predicates, and actions by activity verbs or predicates.

definition: To say or write something clearly as a fact.
example: The report states that the water is safe to drink.
distinctions: State presents a claim clearly; prove requires evidence establishing that the claim is true.

originalSense.definition: To declare to be a fact.
originalSense.example: He stated that he was willing to help.

distinctionTask.prompt: The report _____ that the water is safe, although it gives no supporting evidence.
distinctionTask.explanation: States reports the claim; proves would require evidence establishing it.

definition: To express or make something known explicitly.
example: Please state your reasons for applying.
distinctions: State makes information explicit; imply communicates it indirectly.

originalSense.definition: To make known.
originalSense.example: State your intentions.

definition: Stately: dignified or grand in appearance or manner.
example: In the old phrase “so stiff and so state”, state describes a stately bearing.
distinctions: This adjective means stately; the modern noun state usually names a condition or political entity.
usage: Obsolete adjective. The example modernises the spelling of a phrase in the source example; use stately in modern writing.

originalSense.definition: Stately.
originalSense.example: The ſhepheardes ſwayne you cannot well ken, / But it be by his pride, from other men: / They looken bigge as Bulles, that bene bate, / And bearen the cragge ſo ſtiffe and ſo ſtate, / As Cocke on his dunghill, crowing cranck.

definition: A political entity exercising authority over people within a defined territory.
example: A sovereign state exercises authority within its territory.
distinctions: A state is the political entity; a government is the body that administers it at a particular time.

originalSense.definition: A political entity that regulates society and the population within a definite territory.

definition: The government and public authorities of the country in which someone lives.
example: The state funds compulsory education through taxation.
distinctions: The state refers to public authority; the private sector consists of privately controlled organisations.
usage: Often used with the definite article: the state.

originalSense.definition: The current governing political entity in which the speaker lives.

definition: A shortened reference to a particular State University when the context identifies it.
example: In the sports report, “State” is short for the university’s name.
distinctions: Capitalised State can abbreviate a university name; lowercase state has ordinary political and condition meanings.
usage: A proper name, mainly in US university and sports contexts. The university must be identifiable from context.

originalSense.definition: State University, as the shortened form of a public university name.
originalSense.example: State begins fouling and UCLA misses a couple of front-end free throws on one-and-ones.

definition: An issue, situation or subject that needs attention or consideration.
example: We need to discuss the matter before making a decision.
distinctions: A matter is an issue under consideration; a problem specifically involves a difficulty.
usage: In what is the matter? or something is the matter, the phrase asks about or describes a problem.

originalSense.definition: An affair, condition, or subject, especially one of concern or (especially when preceded by the) one that is problematic.
originalSense.example: Something is the matter with him.

definition: An approximate amount of time, distance or another quantity.
example: The ambulance arrived in a matter of minutes.
collocations: a matter of a few metres
distinctions: A matter of minutes describes an amount or short span; a matter for discussion describes an issue.
usage: Usually a matter of followed by an amount or quantity.

originalSense.definition: An approximate amount or extent.
originalSense.example: I stayed for a matter of months.

definition: A particular issue or case for which a lawyer or law firm provides services.
example: The firm opened a separate file for each legal matter.
distinctions: A legal matter is broader than a court case; it can involve advice or transactions without litigation.
usage: Legal practice.

originalSense.definition: Legal services provided by a lawyer or firm to their client in relation to a particular issue.
originalSense.example: Please find attached an invoice for three outstanding matters.

definition: The essence or embodiment of a quality.
example: The older expression “the matter of virtue” presents someone as the embodiment of virtue.
distinctions: This historical sense means embodiment; a matter of principle in modern English means an issue involving principle.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the source’s older expression; use essence or embodiment in modern writing.

originalSense.definition: Essence; pith; embodiment.
originalSense.example: He is the matter of virtue.

definition: The cause or reason for something, especially something unpleasant.

usage: Formal. Usually condition something on or upon something.

originalSense.definition: To make dependent on a condition to be fulfilled; to make conditional on.
originalSense.example: After some opposition, Marianne yielded to her sister's entreaties, and consented to go out […] She expressly conditioned, however, for paying no visits […]

distinctionTask.prompt: The fund conditioned its support _____ completion of an independent audit.
distinctionTask.explanation: Condition support on an audit makes the audit a requirement; conditioned by describes influence or constraint.

definition: To shape, limit or determine the circumstances in which something happens.
example: Available funding conditions the scope of the research.
distinctions: Condition here means constrain or influence; condition something on an event means make it dependent on that event.
usage: Formal; often used with by in the passive.

originalSense.definition: To place conditions or limitations upon.
originalSense.example: Yet seas that daily gain upon the shore / Have ebb and flow conditioning their march, / And slow and sure comes up the golden year.

definition: To shape a learned response or pattern of behaviour through experience or training.
example: The dog was conditioned to associate the sound with food.
distinctions: Conditioning establishes a learned association or response; an innate reflex does not require learning.
usage: Psychology and behavioural training.

originalSense.definition: To shape the behaviour of someone to do something.
originalSense.example: The children were conditioned to speak up if they had any disagreements.

definition: To treat something to improve its state, especially hair with conditioner.
example: She washed and conditioned her hair before drying it.
distinctions: Conditioning treats or maintains the material; washing primarily removes dirt or unwanted substances.

originalSense.definition: To treat, especially hair with hair conditioner.
originalSense.example: Experiments on steep inclines in the United States showed that washing the rails with a detergent to remove oil and grease resulted in a marked improvement; but conditioning the rails with a special neutralising chemical completely eliminated slipping on a bank on which it was so common as to necessitate restriction of trainloads.

definition: To agree, bargain or stipulate terms.
example: In the older expression “I’ll condition with you”, condition means agree or bargain.
distinctions: This older condition means agree on terms; modern condition funding on approval means make funding dependent on approval.
usage: Archaic. The example modernises and explains the source’s phrase; use agree or stipulate in modern writing.

originalSense.definition: To contract; to stipulate; to agree.
originalSense.example: [P]ay me back my credit, / And I'll condition wi'ye.

definition: To test a textile material, such as silk, to establish its moisture content or commercial weight.
example: The testing house conditioned the silk to determine its moisture content.
distinctions: This specialised conditioning concerns moisture assessment; dyeing changes colour.
usage: Textile testing and historical textile trade. The source records testing silk for moisture content.

originalSense.definition: To test or assay, as silk (to ascertain the proportion of moisture it contains).
originalSense.example: divers parcel of silk conditioned or assayed

definition: To require a student to pass an additional examination or complete work in order to remain enrolled or progress.
example: In older US college usage, to condition a student meant to require additional work or an examination after a failure.
collocations: condition a student (older US college use)
be conditioned in a subject (older use)
distinctions: This educational condition imposes a requirement on continued study; expel removes the student from the institution.
usage: US college terminology, chiefly historical. This example explains the source definition; modern institutions use their own terminology.

originalSense.definition: To put under conditions; to require to pass a new examination or to make up a specified study, as a condition of remaining in one's class or in college.
originalSense.example: to condition a student who has failed in some branch of study

definition: To understand an object by placing it within relations or conditions regarded as necessary for thought.
example: In the source’s philosophical statement “to think is thus to condition”, condition concerns the relations required for knowing an object.
distinctions: This philosophical use concerns the conditions of thought or knowledge; ordinary conditioning concerns training, treatment or dependence.
usage: Philosophy; the meaning depends on the theory being discussed. The example explains the source statement.

originalSense.definition: To impose upon an object those relations or conditions without which knowledge and thought are alleged to be impossible.
originalSense.example: "To think is thus to condition," because it is to know this or that object, and this or that object in a particular mode or condition.

definition: A patient’s state of health at a particular time.
example: The hospital reported that the patient’s condition was stable.
distinctions: A patient’s condition describes their current health status; a diagnosed condition is a particular illness or disorder.
usage: Medical reporting. Stable means not changing substantially; it does not by itself mean well or out of danger.

originalSense.definition: The health status of a medical patient.

distinctionTask.prompt: Doctors reported that the patient’s _____ remained stable overnight.
distinctionTask.explanation: Condition here means current health status; a prerequisite is a prior requirement.

definition: An illness, disorder or other abnormal state of health.
example: She has a long-term heart condition that requires regular monitoring.
distinctions: A condition can be a diagnosed health problem; a symptom is an experience or sign that may indicate one.
usage: Medical and general health contexts.

originalSense.definition: A certain abnormal state of health; a malady or sickness.

definition: A person’s social or economic rank or position.
example: In older writing, a person “of low condition” is of low social rank.
distinctions: Condition here means social rank; in poor condition normally describes health or physical state in modern English.
usage: Obsolete social-rank sense. The example explains the older construction.

originalSense.definition: The situation of a person or persons, particularly their social and/or economic class, rank.

definition: A ladder, series of steps or means of climbing.
example: In obsolete usage, a scale can mean a ladder used for climbing.
distinctions: This obsolete noun means ladder; modern scale a wall is a verb meaning climb it.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the historical definition rather than offering a modern model sentence.

originalSense.definition: A ladder; a series of steps; a means of ascending.

definition: An ordered system of marks or values used to measure or rate something.
example: Please rate the service on a scale from one to five.
distinctions: A scale provides ordered values; a unit is a specified amount used for measurement.

originalSense.definition: An ordered, usually numerical sequence used for measurement; means of assigning a magnitude.
originalSense.example: Please rate your experience on a scale from 1 to 10.

definition: The size, extent or scope of something.
example: The report reveals the scale of the housing shortage.
distinctions: Scale concerns size or extent; rate concerns a quantity relative to another quantity, often time.

originalSense.definition: Size; scope.
originalSense.example: There are some who question the scale of our ambitions.

definition: The ratio between a distance in a representation and the corresponding real distance.
example: At a scale of 1:50,000, one centimetre on the map represents 500 metres on the ground.
distinctions: A ratio scale compares lengths in the same units; a scale bar labels a distance graphically.
usage: Maps, plans and models. A larger-scale map has a larger representative fraction and usually shows a smaller area in more detail.

originalSense.definition: The ratio of depicted distance to actual distance.
originalSense.example: This map uses a scale of 1:10.

distinctionTask.prompt: A map’s _____ of 1:50,000 means that one centimetre represents 500 metres.
distinctionTask.explanation: Scale compares represented distance with real distance; range describes extent, limits or reach.

definition: A labelled line or bar on a drawing or image showing the distance represented.
example: The micrograph includes a scale bar representing ten micrometres.
collocations: include a scale in the image
distinctions: A scale bar remains proportional when the whole image is resized; a written magnification value may no longer be correct after resizing.
usage: Maps, drawings and scientific images.

originalSense.definition: A line or bar associated with a drawing, used to indicate measurement when the image has been magnified or reduced.
originalSense.example: Even though precision can be carried to an extreme, the scales which now are drawn in (and usually connected to an appropriate figure by an arrow) will allow derivation of meaningful measurements.

definition: An ordered series of musical pitches, usually arranged within an octave or another repeating interval.
example: The pianist practised a C major scale.
distinctions: A scale orders pitches; a chord combines pitches sounded together or understood as a harmony.
usage: Music. Not every musical scale uses an octave as its repeating interval.

originalSense.definition: A series of notes spanning an octave, tritave, or pseudo-octave, used to make melodies.

definition: The base or radix of a numeral system.
example: The older term “binary scale” refers to a numeral system with base two.
distinctions: The base determines place values; the digits are the symbols used to express numbers in that base.
usage: Mathematics; base or radix is more usual in modern terminology.

originalSense.definition: A mathematical base for a numeral system; radix.
originalSense.example: the decimal scale, the binary scale

definition: A graduated series of levels, ranks or degrees.
example: The course moves through a scale of increasing difficulty.
distinctions: A scale orders degrees or levels; a list need not imply any ranking.

originalSense.definition: Gradation; succession of ascending and descending steps and degrees; progressive series; scheme of comparative rank or order.
originalSense.example: There is a certain scale of duties […] which for want of studying in right order, all the world is in confusion.

definition: A standard or negotiated rate of pay for a particular kind of work.
example: The actor was paid scale for the television appearance.
distinctions: Scale is the standard rate in this use; a fee is the actual payment agreed for a job.
usage: Especially US entertainment-industry and union contexts.

originalSense.definition: A standard amount of money to be paid for a service, for example union-negotiated amounts received by a performer or writer; similar to wage scale or pay grade.
originalSense.example: Sally wasn't the star of the show, so she was glad to be paid scale.

definition: To change size or output, often by applying a proportional factor.
example: The designer scaled the drawing to twice its original width and height.
distinctions: Scaling every length by two makes a flat shape’s area four times as large; the linear and area factors differ.
usage: Design, mathematics and production. In scaling a process, capacity may change without every physical dimension changing proportionally.

originalSense.definition: To change the size of something whilst maintaining proportion; especially to change a process in order to produce much larger amounts of the final product.
originalSense.example: We should scale that up by a factor of 10.

distinctionTask.prompt: If all lengths in a flat shape are doubled, its area becomes _____ times as large.
distinctionTask.explanation: Area changes with the square of the linear factor: 2 × 2 = 4.

definition: To climb to the top of a high or steep surface.
example: The climbers scaled the steep rock face before noon.
distinctions: Scale takes the obstacle as its object; climb can also describe moving up a ladder, stairs or slope more generally.

originalSense.definition: To climb to the top of.
originalSense.example: Hilary and Norgay were the first known to have scaled Everest.

definition: To remain workable as demand, throughput or size increases.
example: The service must scale to support thousands of simultaneous users.
distinctions: A system scales if it can handle growth; a system can be fast at a small workload and still scale poorly.
usage: Business and computing; intransitive.

originalSense.definition: To tolerate significant increases in throughput or other potentially limiting factors.
originalSense.example: That architecture won't scale to real-world environments.

definition: To handle a substantially increasing workload without failing.
example: The database scaled as the number of daily requests increased.
distinctions: Scale concerns behaviour as workload grows; availability concerns whether the service can be used at a given time.
usage: Computing and systems engineering. This overlaps the broader scalability meaning but preserves its distinct source ID.

originalSense.definition: To handle heavily increasing loads without breaking down.
originalSense.example: We started using the term “scaling” in place of “growing” around the late 1990s to early 2000s, primarily due to the rise of venture-backed startups in Silicon Valley. The term migrated from tech/infrastructure (“can this system scale?”) to startups (“can this business scale?”)

definition: To grow revenue or output without a proportional increase in costs.
example: The software business aims to scale by serving more customers without matching increases in staffing costs.
distinctions: Scaling in this business sense emphasises costs growing more slowly than revenue; simple growth does not imply that relationship.
usage: Entrepreneurship and business. The source describes exponential revenue growth; actual growth is not guaranteed by the word.

originalSense.definition: To increase revenues exponentially without proportional increases in costs.
originalSense.example: We started using the term “scaling” in place of “growing” around the late 1990s to early 2000s, primarily due to the rise of venture-backed startups in Silicon Valley. [...] VCs needed a way to describe businesses that could grow exponentially without adding proportional headcount or expense. So scalability became the holy grail. The term migrated from tech/infrastructure (“can this system scale?”) to startups (“can this business scale?”) and now everyone from lifestyle brands to DTC businesses use it as a universal term for "make business go big." (By the mid-2010s, “scale” was in every pitch deck and founder tweet, even if what they really meant was: “We’re trying to 𝘨𝘳𝘰𝘸, but we want to sound smarter so we're using the term "scale".”) This change in language actually had a HUGE effect on the minds of the people who were operating businesses across the globe.

definition: To measure, weigh or grade something using a scale or system.
example: The examiner scaled the scores to a common standard.
distinctions: Scale applies a measurement or grading system; compare can describe a broader judgement without assigning values.

originalSense.definition: To weigh, measure or grade according to a scale or system.
originalSense.example: Scaling his present bearing with his past.

definition: To derive a measurement from a drawing by using its scale.
example: The engineer checked the written dimensions rather than scaling the drawing.
distinctions: Scaling derives dimensions from the representation; written dimensions specify intended values directly.
usage: Engineering drawings. “Do not scale” means do not infer dimensions by measuring the drawing.

originalSense.definition: To take measurements from (an engineering drawing), treating them as (or as if) reliable dimensional instructions.
originalSense.example: Every single drawing in the specification has a warning in its title block which reads, "Do not scale this drawing."

definition: One of the small protective plates covering the skin of many fish, reptiles and other animals.
example: The fish’s scales overlapped along its body.
distinctions: Scales are protective structures; their composition varies. Many fish scales contain mineralised tissue, whereas reptile scales are keratinised skin.
usage: Zoology. Fish and reptile scales should not all be described as pieces of keratin.

originalSense.definition: Part of an overlapping arrangement of many small, flat and hard pieces of keratin covering the skin of an animal, particularly a fish or reptile.
originalSense.example: Fish that, with their fins and shining scales, / Glide under the green wave.

definition: A tiny flattened chitinous structure covering a butterfly’s or moth’s wings.
example: Under the microscope, individual scales covered the butterfly’s wing.
distinctions: Insect wing scales are modified hair-like structures; fish scales are different protective structures.
usage: Entomology. Wing colour can arise from pigments, microscopic structure or both.

originalSense.definition: A small piece of pigmented chitin, many of which coat the wings of a butterfly or moth to give them their color.

definition: A flake of skin shed from a surface, especially one affected by a skin disorder.
example: The dermatologist observed fine scales on the affected skin.
distinctions: A scale is a flake of skin; a scab is dried material formed over a wound.
usage: Dermatology.

originalSense.definition: A flake of skin of an animal afflicted with dermatitis.

definition: One of the overlapping protective structures of a cone, such as a pine cone.
example: The pine cone’s scales opened as it dried.
distinctions: Cone scales protect or bear the seeds; they are not themselves seeds.
usage: Botany.

originalSense.definition: Part of an overlapping arrangement of many small, flat and hard protective layers forming a pinecone that flare when mature to release pine nut seeds.

definition: A flaky layer, especially oxide, formed on heated metal.
example: The rolling process removed loose scale from the steel.
distinctions: Metal scale is usually an oxide layer; rust is corrosion associated specifically with iron and its alloys.
usage: Metallurgy.

originalSense.definition: The flaky material sloughed off heated metal.

definition: Armour made from small overlapping plates attached to a backing.
example: The museum displayed scale armour beside a suit of mail.
distinctions: Scale armour uses overlapping plates on a backing; chain mail uses interlinked rings.
usage: Historical armour; scale mail is another name for scale armour.

originalSense.definition: Scale mail (as opposed to chain mail).

definition: A hard mineral deposit left by water, especially on heated surfaces.
example: Hard water left a layer of scale inside the kettle.
distinctions: Scale is the mineral deposit; hard water contains dissolved minerals that can form it.
usage: Usually uncountable in this meaning.

originalSense.definition: Limescale.

distinctionTask.prompt: Hard water left a mineral deposit called _____ inside the kettle.
distinctionTask.explanation: Scale is the deposited mineral material; soil is earth in which plants may grow.

definition: A scale insect: a small plant-feeding insect, often protected by a waxy covering.
example: The gardener found scale on the underside of the leaves.
distinctions: A scale insect is an animal pest; a fungal infection is caused by a fungus.
usage: Entomology and gardening.

originalSense.definition: A scale insect.

definition: A thin side plate forming part of a pocketknife handle.
example: The restorer replaced a damaged scale on the pocketknife handle.
distinctions: A handle scale forms an outer side of the handle; a liner is a separate internal supporting plate.
usage: Knife construction; the source specifically records a thin metallic side plate.

originalSense.definition: The thin metallic side plate of the handle of a pocketknife.

definition: An infestation of scale insects on a plant.
example: The nursery inspected the citrus trees for scale.
distinctions: Scale here is an insect infestation; it should not be assumed to be a plant disease caused by a pathogen.
usage: Gardening and plant protection; recorded as US usage in the source.

originalSense.definition: An infestation of scale insects on a plant; commonly thought of as, or mistaken for, a disease.
originalSense.example: Although of no effect so far as the course of the small outbreak at Nacaugai is concerned it is necessary to add here that the prompt destruction of kavika trees over much of the neighbouring land on Nagasau estate was in all probability an important measure of control and responsible for the freedom from scale of Nagasau estate at the time when Mua was badly attacked.

definition: To remove scales from a fish or another surface.
example: The cook scaled the fish before cleaning it.
distinctions: Scale removes the external scales; gut removes the internal organs.
usage: Transitive.

originalSense.definition: To remove the scales of.
originalSense.example: Please scale that fish for dinner.

distinctionTask.prompt: Before removing its internal organs, the cook used a scraper to _____ the fish.
distinctionTask.explanation: Scale removes external scales; gut removes the internal organs.

definition: To develop or shed small flakes or scales on a surface.
example: The dry skin began to scale.
distinctions: Scale describes flaking or becoming scaly; scar describes the formation of lasting repair tissue.
usage: Intransitive; often used of skin.

originalSense.definition: To become scaly; to produce or develop scales.
originalSense.example: The dry weather is making my skin scale.

definition: To remove a layer or deposit in thin flakes, including tartar from teeth.
example: The hygienist scaled the teeth to remove hardened deposits.
distinctions: Scaling removes hardened deposits; polishing smooths a surface after cleaning.
usage: Transitive; dentistry and surface treatment.

originalSense.definition: To take off in thin layers or scales, as tartar from the teeth; to pare off, as a surface.
originalSense.example:
1684-1690, Thomas Burnet, Sacred Theory of the Earth
if all the mountains and hills were scaled, and the earth made even

definition: To separate or come off in thin layers or flakes.
example: The weathered stone began to scale at the edges.
distinctions: Scale describes thin layers separating; crack describes a break that need not detach a layer.
usage: Intransitive; materials and surfaces.

originalSense.definition: To separate and come off in thin layers or laminae.
originalSense.example: Some sandstone scales by exposure.

definition: To scatter or spread.
example: In Scots dialect, scale can mean scatter or spread.
distinctions: This dialect scale means scatter; scale up in standard modern English means increase size or capacity.
usage: Scots or northern British dialect. The example explains the regional meaning rather than quoting an attested sentence.

originalSense.definition: To scatter; to spread.

definition: To clean the inside of a cannon by firing a small charge of powder.
example: The older account describes cannons being scaled before they were loaded.
distinctions: This historical artillery verb describes cleaning; scale a wall describes climbing.
usage: Historical artillery. The example paraphrases the source’s “scaled and loaded” wording; it is not an operating instruction.

originalSense.definition: To clean, as the inside of a cannon, by the explosion of a small quantity of powder.
originalSense.example: cannons […]caused to be scaled and loaded

definition: An instrument used to measure mass or weight.
example: The parcel weighed two kilograms on the digital scale.
distinctions: A scale is the measuring instrument; a kilogram is a unit of mass.
usage: Singular scale is common in American English; British English often uses scales for the whole instrument.

originalSense.definition: A device to measure mass or weight.
originalSense.example: After the long, lazy winter I was afraid to get on the scale.

definition: One of the pans or trays of a balance.
example: The jeweller placed the stone in one scale and the reference weights in the other.
distinctions: A scale here is one pan; scales can refer to the complete weighing instrument.
usage: Especially descriptions of a two-pan balance.

originalSense.definition: Either of the pans, trays, or dishes of a balance or scales.

definition: A cooking stove, especially a large one with several burners and often an oven.
example: The chef heated the soup on the gas range.
distinctions: A range is a cooking appliance; an oven is its enclosed heated compartment or a separate appliance.
usage: The cooking-stove sense is especially common in American English. Older uses include a fireplace or other cooking apparatus.

originalSense.definition: A fireplace; a fire or other cooking apparatus; now specifically, a large cooking stove with many burners (hotplates).
originalSense.example: Therein an hundred raunges weren pight, / And hundred fournaces all burning bright; / By euery fournace many feendes did byde, / Deformed creatures, horrible in ſight, / And euery feend his buſie paines applyde, / To melt the golden metall, ready to be tryde.

definition: A variety or selection of related things.
example: The library offers a wide range of online courses.
distinctions: Range emphasises variety or breadth; quantity describes how much or how many there are.

originalSense.definition: Selection, array.
originalSense.example: We sell a wide range of cars.

definition: An area set aside for practising shooting at targets.
example: The club held its target practice at the indoor range.
distinctions: A range is the designated practice area; a target is the object aimed at.

originalSense.definition: An area for practicing shooting at targets.

definition: An area used for military training or equipment testing.
example: The vehicle was evaluated on the army’s test range.
distinctions: A test range is a controlled testing area; range can also mean how far equipment can operate.
usage: Military training and testing.

originalSense.definition: An area for military training or equipment testing.

definition: The distance from an observer or sensor to an object or event.
example: The radar measured the aircraft’s range as twenty kilometres.
distinctions: Range is the distance to the object; bearing is its direction from the observer.
usage: Measurement, radar and navigation.

originalSense.definition: The distance from a person or sensor to an object, target, emanation, or event.
originalSense.example: We could see the ship at a range of five miles.

definition: The maximum distance over which something can operate, reach or be detected.
example: The transmitter has a range of about five kilometres.
distinctions: Range is maximum reach in this use; signal strength can vary at different distances within that reach.

originalSense.definition: The maximum distance or reach of capability (of a weapon, radio, detector, etc.).
originalSense.example: This missile's range is 500 kilometres.

definition: The distance a vehicle can travel before it needs more fuel or stored energy.
example: The electric car has an estimated range of three hundred kilometres on a full charge.
distinctions: Range measures distance before refuelling or recharging; efficiency compares distance travelled with energy used.
usage: Actual range depends on conditions such as speed, temperature, terrain and load.

originalSense.definition: The distance a vehicle (e.g., a car, bicycle, lorry, or aircraft) can travel without refueling.
originalSense.example: This aircraft's range is 15 000 kilometres.

definition: Open land used for grazing animals, often without fences.
example: The cattle grazed on the open range.
distinctions: Range is grazing country; a cultivated field is land prepared for crops.
usage: Especially North American ranching and land management.

originalSense.definition: An area of open, often unfenced, grazing land.
originalSense.example: There is a young cowboy, he lives on the range / His horse and his cattle are his only companions

definition: The extent, limits or scope within which something operates or varies.
example: The instrument measures temperatures across a wide range.
distinctions: Range describes an extent or set of limits; the statistical range specifically equals the maximum minus the minimum.

originalSense.definition: The extent or space taken in by anything excursive; compass or extent of excursion; reach; scope.
originalSense.example: As to acquir’d habits and abilities in Learning, his Writings having given the World ſufficient account of them, there remains onely to obſerve, that the range and compaſs of his knowledge fill’d the whole Circle of the Arts, and reach’d thoſe ſeverals which ſingle do exact an entire man unto themſelves, and full age.

definition: The set of output values actually attained by a function on its domain.
example: For f(x) = x² with real x, the range is all real numbers greater than or equal to zero.
distinctions: The domain contains allowed inputs; the range contains outputs actually reached. A codomain can contain values that are never reached.
usage: Mathematics. Some texts use range for codomain, so check the author’s convention; here it means the image.

originalSense.definition: The set of values (points) which a function can obtain.

distinctionTask.prompt: For f(x) = x² on the real numbers, negative inputs belong to the _____ but negative outputs do not occur.
distinctionTask.explanation: The domain contains inputs; the range contains outputs actually attained, which are nonnegative for real x².

definition: The difference between the largest and smallest observations in a data set.
example: For the data 2, 5 and 9, the range is 9 − 2 = 7.
distinctions: Range measures the full spread from smallest to largest; an average describes a central value.
usage: Statistics. The range is sensitive to extreme observations.

originalSense.definition: The length of the smallest interval which contains all the data in a sample; the difference between the largest and smallest observations in the sample.

distinctionTask.prompt: For the observations 2, 5 and 9, the _____ is 7.
distinctionTask.explanation: The range is 9 − 2 = 7. The mean is (2 + 5 + 9) ÷ 3, which is not 7.

definition: The area a defensive player is able to cover.
example: The shortstop’s range allowed her to reach balls far to either side.
distinctions: A player’s range is the area they can cover; their fielding position is the role or starting location.
usage: Sport, especially baseball.

originalSense.definition: The defensive area that a player can cover.
originalSense.example: Jones has good range for a big man.

definition: The span of pitches a voice or musical instrument can produce.
example: The singer chose a song that suited her vocal range.
distinctions: Range concerns the lowest to highest available pitches; a scale is a particular ordered series of pitches.
usage: Music.

originalSense.definition: The scale of all the tones a voice or an instrument can produce.

definition: The geographical area in which a species naturally occurs.
example: The survey mapped the species’ range across the region.
distinctions: Range describes geographical distribution; habitat describes the type of environment in which an organism lives.
usage: Ecology and biogeography.

originalSense.definition: The geographical area or zone where a species is normally naturally found.

distinctionTask.prompt: The geographical area where a species naturally occurs is its _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Range is geographical distribution; habitat type describes the environment, such as woodland or wetland.

definition: A sequence of values specified by bounds or an iteration rule.
example: In Python, range(1, 4) represents the integers 1, 2 and 3.
distinctions: A Python range is an iterable sequence object, not a materialised list or itself an iterator; iter(range(...)) produces an iterator.
usage: Programming. Whether an endpoint is included depends on the language or operation; Python excludes the stop value.

originalSense.definition: A sequential list of values specified by an iterator.
originalSense.example: std::for_each calls the given function on each value in the input range.

distinctionTask.prompt: In Python, range(1, 4) includes 1, 2 and 3, and stops before _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Python excludes the stop value, so 4 is not included; 3 is included.

definition: A class or group of individuals sharing a rank or degree.
example: In older usage, a range can mean a class of people at the same rank.
collocations: a range meaning a rank or class (older use)
distinctions: This older range classifies individuals by rank; a modern range of people emphasises variety.
usage: Uncommon older classification sense. The example explains the dictionary definition.

originalSense.definition: An aggregate of individuals in one rank or degree; an order; a class.
originalSense.example: The next Range of Beings above him are the pure and immaterial Intelligences , the next below him is the sensible Nature.

definition: A rung or step of a ladder.
example: In obsolete usage, a range can mean one rung of a ladder.
distinctions: A rung is one step; a ladder is the complete structure.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the historical definition; use rung in modern English.

originalSense.definition: The step of a ladder; a rung.
originalSense.example: the first range of that ladder

definition: A sieve used to sift flour or meal.
example: In older British dialect, range could name a bolting sieve for meal.
distinctions: This historical range is a sifting tool; a modern kitchen range is a cooking appliance.
usage: Obsolete British dialect. The example explains the source definition rather than recommending the word for a modern tool.

originalSense.definition: A bolting sieve to sift meal.

definition: An act of wandering or travelling to and fro; a ramble or excursion.
example: In older travel writing, a range can mean a ramble through the countryside.
collocations: a range meaning a ramble (older use)
distinctions: This noun names an excursion; the verb range describes roaming.
usage: Uncommon or older noun. The example explains the reading sense.

originalSense.definition: A wandering or roving; a going to and fro; an excursion; a ramble; an expedition.
originalSense.example:
, "Taking Pleasure in Other Men's Sins"
He may take a range all the world over.

definition: A north–south tier of townships in the US public land survey system.
example: The deed identifies the parcel as lying in Township 3 North, Range 2 West.
distinctions: A range is identified east or west of a principal meridian; a township is identified north or south of a baseline.
usage: US land-survey terminology. Range lines are nominally six miles apart, with survey corrections and exceptions.

originalSense.definition: In the public land system, a row or line of townships lying between two succession meridian lines six miles apart.

definition: The variety of roles, styles or emotions a performer can portray convincingly.
example: Her work in both comedy and tragedy demonstrates her range as an actor.
distinctions: Acting range concerns versatility; vocal range concerns the span of pitches a voice can produce.

originalSense.definition: The variety of roles that an actor can play in a satisfactory way.
originalSense.example: By playing in comedies as well as in dramas he has proved his range as an actor.

definition: To roam or travel around an area.
example: The deer ranged across the open hills.
distinctions: Range describes movement over an area; remain describes staying in one place.
usage: Intransitive.

originalSense.definition: To travel over (an area, etc); to roam, wander.

definition: To roam through or over a place.
example: The walkers ranged the hills in search of the old path.
distinctions: Range takes the area as its direct object here; wander usually uses a preposition such as through or over.
usage: Transitive; often literary.

originalSense.definition: To rove over or through.
originalSense.example: to range the fields

definition: To bring something under a power or make it conform to something else.
example: In the source phrase “rangeth to her selfe”, range means bring something under the soul’s influence.
collocations: rangeth to her selfe (obsolete source wording)
distinctions: This obsolete range concerns power or submission; the modern verb usually describes extent, variation or roaming.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the source’s older construction; it is not a model for modern prose.

originalSense.definition: To exercise the power of something over something else; to cause to submit to, over.
originalSense.example: The soule is variable in all manner of formes, and rangeth to her selfe, and to her estate, whatsoever it be, the senses of the body, and all other accidents.

definition: To bring or place something in a specified position or relationship to something else.
example: The commanders ranged their forces against the opposing army.
distinctions: Range can position people or things relative to others; arrange is the broader everyday verb for putting things in order.
usage: Formal. The source also records intransitive use in “ranging alongside”.

originalSense.definition: To bring (something) into a specified position or relationship (especially, of opposition) with something else.
originalSense.example: At last we gained such an offing, that the two pilots were needed no longer. The stout sail-boat that had accompanied us began ranging alongside.

definition: To vary or take values within specified limits.
example: The values of x range from zero to ten.
distinctions: Use from with to, and between with and. Range states limits or possible variation; average states a central value.
usage: Variables, measurements and other changing quantities.

originalSense.definition: Of a variable, to be able to take any of the values in a specified range.
originalSense.example: The variable x ranges over all real values from 0 to 10.

definition: To place things into classes or categories.
example: The older classification ranges the plants into genera and species.
distinctions: Range here means classify; a numerical range describes values or limits.
usage: Formal or older classificatory use; classify is more usual today.

originalSense.definition: To classify.
originalSense.example: to range plants and animals in genera and species

definition: To form a line or align with something.
example: The front of the house ranges with the street.
distinctions: Range describes alignment in this use; range across a region describes movement or extent.
usage: Uncommon formal or architectural use; intransitive.

originalSense.definition: To form a line or a row.
originalSense.example: The front of a house ranges with the street.

definition: To belong in an order, rank or class.
example: In older usage, to range with others can mean to rank or be classed with them.
distinctions: This range concerns membership of a rank or class; range over an area concerns movement.
usage: Uncommon or older intransitive use. The example explains the source definition.

originalSense.definition: To be placed in order; to be ranked; to admit of arrangement or classification; to rank.
originalSense.example: And range with humble livers in content.

definition: To arrange people or things in a line, row or ordered formation.
example: The attendant ranged the chairs in neat rows.
distinctions: Range is transitive when someone arranges the objects; the objects range along a wall is intransitive.
usage: Formal; arrange is more usual in everyday speech.

originalSense.definition: To set in a row, or in rows; to place in a regular line or lines, or in ranks; to dispose in the proper order.
originalSense.example: Maccabeus ranged his army by hands.

definition: To place oneself with a group or on one side of a dispute.
example: She ranged herself on the side of the reformers.
collocations: range oneself on the side of
distinctions: Range oneself with a group means align with it; simply stand beside someone need not imply support.
usage: Formal or literary; often reflexive.

originalSense.definition: To place among others in a line, row, or order, as in the ranks of an army; usually, reflexively and figuratively, to espouse a cause, to join a party, etc.
originalSense.example: It would be absurd in me to range myself on the side of the Duke of Bedford and the corresponding society.

definition: To occur naturally across a particular geographical area.
example: The species ranges from the coast to the inland mountains.
distinctions: A species ranges across its distribution area; an individual animal roams within an area.
usage: Biology and biogeography.

originalSense.definition: To be native to, or live in, a certain district or region.
originalSense.example: The peba ranges from Texas to Paraguay.

definition: To determine the distance to a target.
example: The radar system ranged the target before tracking its movement.
distinctions: Ranging determines distance; finding a bearing determines direction.
usage: Military, surveying and sensor terminology.

originalSense.definition: To determine the range to a target.

definition: To sail or move along or close to something.
example: The survey vessel ranged the coast throughout the summer.
distinctions: Range the coast means travel along it; cross the sea means move from one side to another.
usage: Nautical or literary.

originalSense.definition: To sail or pass in a direction parallel to or near.
originalSense.example: to range the coast

definition: To move a considerable distance to make a defensive play.
example: The shortstop ranged to her left to stop the ball.
distinctions: Range describes the defensive movement; the catch or throw is the subsequent action.
usage: Baseball.

originalSense.definition: Of a player, to travel a significant distance for a defensive play.
originalSense.example: Willie, playing in left-center, raced toward a ball no human had any business getting a glove to. Mays ranged to his left, searching, digging in, pouring on the speed, as the crowd screamed its anticipation of a triple.

definition: A family name.
example: Ms Range signed the letter.
distinctions: Capitalised Range can be a surname; lowercase range has separate ordinary noun and verb meanings.
usage: Proper name. The example is illustrative and makes no claim about a particular person.

originalSense.definition: A surname.

definition: A place name used for communities in Alabama, Ohio and Wisconsin, and for a township in Ohio, United States.
example: The directory lists Range in Madison County, Ohio.
distinctions: Range here is a place name; include the state or county to distinguish the different locations.
usage: Proper name. The source lists a community in Conecuh County, Alabama; a township and community in Madison County, Ohio; and a community in Polk County, Wisconsin.

originalSense.definition: A place in the United States:

definition: The surface of the earth, especially the surface under your feet.
example: She put the heavy bag down on the ground.
distinctions: Ground is the earth’s surface; floor usually means the lower surface inside a building.
usage: Usually uncountable in this meaning.

originalSense.definition: The surface of the Earth, as opposed to the sky or water or underground.
originalSense.example: Look, I found a ten dollar bill on the ground!

definition: Land considered in terms of its surface, shape or suitability for an activity.
example: The rescue team crossed steep, rocky ground.
distinctions: Ground describes terrain here; soil describes the material in which plants can grow.

originalSense.definition: Terrain.
originalSense.example: As the terrain-following radar scans the ground ahead of the aircraft the actual clearance height is measured by the radio altimeter.

definition: Soil or earth as a material.
example: The gardener planted the seedlings in moist ground.
