distinctions: Ground is earth or soil in this use; a floor is a constructed surface.

originalSense.definition: Soil, earth.
originalSense.example: The worm crawls through the ground.

definition: The bottom of a river, lake, sea or other body of water.
example: The boat touched ground in the shallow channel.
distinctions: Ground here is the underwater bottom; shore is the land along the water’s edge.
usage: Nautical.

originalSense.definition: The bottom of a body of water.

definition: A basis or foundation on which something depends or develops.
example: The agreement provided common ground for further negotiations.
distinctions: Ground provides a basis; a conclusion is what an argument seeks to establish.
usage: Often figurative.

originalSense.definition: Basis, foundation, groundwork, legwork.
originalSense.example:
Wyth cry unreverent,
Before the sacrament,
Wythin the holy church bowndis,
That of our fayth the grownd is.

definition: A reason or justification for an action, belief or decision.
example: There are reasonable grounds for requesting a further inspection.
distinctions: Grounds are reasons or supporting circumstances; a proof establishes a conclusion to the required standard.
usage: Usually plural: grounds. Use grounds for followed by a noun or grounds that followed by a clause.

originalSense.definition: Reason, (epistemic) justification, cause.
originalSense.example: You will need to show good grounds for your action.

distinctionTask.prompt: The inspection found reasonable _____ for concern about the roof.
distinctionTask.explanation: Grounds for concern means supporting reasons; floors are surfaces or levels in a building.

definition: The background, context or framework against which something is considered.
example: The debate took place on the familiar ground of national identity.
distinctions: Ground can be the context or area of discussion; a specific claim is a statement made within it.
usage: Often figurative or formal.

originalSense.definition: Background, context, framework, surroundings.

definition: An area of a battlefield held, gained or lost by a side.
example: The defenders gave ground as the opposing force advanced.
distinctions: Give ground literally means retreat from a position; figuratively it can mean concede an advantage or argument.
usage: Military context; the source labels this battlefield sense historical.

originalSense.definition: The area on which a battle is fought, particularly as referring to the area occupied by one side or the other. Often, according to the eventualities, "to give ground" or "to gain ground".

definition: An advantage or position gained or lost in a contest or dispute.
example: The proposal gained ground as more members expressed support.
distinctions: Gain ground means become stronger or more accepted; gain the ground can describe taking a physical area in a particular context.
usage: Figurative.

originalSense.definition: Advantage given or gained in any contest; e.g. in football, chess, debate or academic discourse.

definition: A place used or suited to a particular activity.
example: The sheltered bay is an important breeding ground for seals.
distinctions: A ground is a place associated with an activity; the activity itself is breeding, hunting or training.
usage: Usually in combinations such as breeding ground or training ground.

originalSense.definition: A place suited to a specified activity.
originalSense.example: a forest traditionally used as a hunting-ground

definition: The background surface on which a design or artistic composition is set.
example: The fabric has red flowers on a white ground.
distinctions: The ground is the background; the figure or motif is the design placed against it.
usage: Art, design and textiles.

originalSense.definition: The plain surface upon which the figures of an artistic composition are set.
originalSense.example: crimson flowers on a white ground

definition: The background surface from which sculpted figures project in relief.
example: The carved leaves stand out from a flat ground.
distinctions: The ground is the background plane; relief is the projection of the figures from it.
usage: Sculpture.

originalSense.definition: A flat surface upon which figures are raised in relief.

definition: The mesh or net background supporting a lace pattern.
example: The lace has delicate floral motifs on a fine mesh ground.
distinctions: The ground is the supporting mesh; the motifs form the visible ornamental pattern.
usage: Lace-making.

originalSense.definition: The net of small meshes upon which the embroidered pattern is applied.
originalSense.example: Brussels ground

definition: An acid-resistant coating applied to a metal plate before etching.
example: The artist drew through the ground to expose lines on the copper plate.
distinctions: The ground protects covered metal from the acid; exposed lines are etched where the coating has been removed.
usage: Etching and printmaking.

originalSense.definition: A gummy substance spread over the surface of a metal to be etched, to prevent the acid from eating except where an opening is made by the needle.

definition: A timber fixing strip set flush with plaster to support mouldings or other fittings.
example: The carpenter fixed the moulding to timber grounds set into the wall.
distinctions: Grounds provide fixing points for fittings; plaster forms the surrounding finished surface.
usage: Traditional building terminology; usually plural.

originalSense.definition: One of the pieces of wood, flush with the plastering, to which mouldings etc. are attached.
originalSense.example: Grounds are usually put up first and the plastering floated flush with them.

definition: A football stadium or the home venue of a club.
example: The supporters arrived at the club’s ground an hour before kick-off.
distinctions: The ground can mean the whole venue; the pitch is the playing surface.
usage: British English, especially association football.

originalSense.definition: A soccer stadium.
originalSense.example: Manchester United's ground is known as Old Trafford.

definition: An electrical connection or conductor used as an earth connection or a reference potential.
example: The circuit diagram marks the common reference node as ground.
distinctions: Signal ground is a reference node and need not connect to the earth; protective earth serves a safety function.
usage: Electrical engineering; earth is also used, especially in British English. These roles must not be assumed interchangeable.

originalSense.definition: An electrical conductor connected to the earth, or a large conductor whose electrical potential is taken as zero (such as a steel chassis).
originalSense.example: А ground may be undesirable, inadvertent, or accidental path taken by an electrical current; or it may be the deliberate provision of conductors well connected to the ground by means of plates buried therein, or similar device.

definition: An electric shock.
example: In the dictionary’s Philippine English entry, ground can mean an electric shock.
distinctions: This regional ground is a shock; in standard electrical terminology a ground is a connection or reference potential.
usage: Philippine English. The example explains the recorded regional sense; use electric shock for an international audience.

originalSense.definition: Electric shock.

definition: A cricket field or venue, or the area behind a batter’s popping crease that counts as their ground.
example: The batter slid the bat behind the crease to make her ground.
distinctions: A cricket ground can be the whole venue; a batter’s ground is the protected area associated with a crease.
usage: Cricket. Run-out decisions depend on the laws governing whether a bat or part of the body is grounded behind the crease.

originalSense.definition: The area of grass on which a match is played (a cricket field); the entire arena in which it is played; the part of the field behind a batsman's popping crease where he can not be run out (hence to make one's ground).

definition: A musical composition based on a repeating bass pattern beneath a changing melody.
example: The ensemble performed a ground built over a repeating bass line.
distinctions: A ground repeats a bass pattern; the melody above it can vary.
usage: Music.

originalSense.definition: A composition in which the bass, consisting of a few bars of independent notes, is continually repeated to a varying melody.

definition: A basic tune or plainsong above which a descant is sung or composed.
example: The composer added a descant above the plain ground.
collocations: build a descant on a ground
distinctions: The ground is the underlying tune; a descant is a higher counter-melody above it.
usage: Older musical terminology.

originalSense.definition: The tune on which descants are raised; the plain song.
originalSense.example: Buck[ingham] The Mayor is here at hand; pretend ſome fear, // Be not you ſpoke with, but by mighty ſuit; // And look you get a prayer-book in your hand, // And ſtand between two churchmen, good my lord, // For on that ground I’ll build a holy deſcant: // And be not eaſily won to our requeſts: // Play the maid’s part, ſtill anſwer nay, and take it.

definition: The pit or lower audience area of a theatre.
example: In the older theatrical phrase “gentlemen of the ground”, ground means the pit where spectators stood or sat.
collocations: the ground of a theatre (older use)
distinctions: The ground is the audience area in this historical use; the stage is where the performers act.
usage: Historical theatre. The example explains a phrase in the source.

originalSense.definition: The pit of a theatre.
originalSense.example: the understanding gentlemen o' the ground here ask'd my judgment

definition: A historical land-area unit used in India, also called a munny.
example: The historical survey recorded the building plot’s area in grounds.
distinctions: A ground is an area unit here; ground in ordinary English names land or its surface without specifying an area.
usage: Historical Indian land measure. The source describes a Madras building ground as one twenty-fourth of a cawny; local units and conventions can vary.

originalSense.definition: Synonym of munny (“land measure”).
originalSense.example: It is sub-divided into annas (or 16ths), of 3,600 square feet each; or when the land is for building purposes, into grounds (munnies) of 1/24 of a cawny each, as in the town of Madras.

definition: To connect electrical equipment or a conductor to earth or to a specified reference conductor.
example: The electrician grounded the metal enclosure through its protective conductor.
distinctions: Grounding establishes the specified electrical connection; it does not simply mean turning equipment off.
usage: Especially American English; British English often uses earth. Protective grounding and signal-reference connections have different purposes.

originalSense.definition: To connect (an electrical conductor or device) to a ground.
originalSense.example: These geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) can become a hazard when they flow through conducting infrastructure, usually entering and exiting networks where equipment is grounded to Earth.

definition: To electrocute.
example: The dictionary records ground meaning electrocute in Philippine English.
distinctions: This regional verb concerns electric injury; ground electrical equipment normally means connect it to earth or a reference conductor.
usage: Philippine English. The example explains the recorded definition rather than offering an everyday model; use an explicit description of the electric injury for clarity.

originalSense.definition: To electrocute.

definition: To punish a child or teenager by restricting outings or other privileges.
example: Her parents grounded her for a week after she broke their agreement.
distinctions: Grounding restricts privileges; it is not the same as physically restraining someone.
usage: Often passive: she is grounded.

originalSense.definition: To punish, especially a child or teenager, by forcing them to stay at home and/or give up certain privileges.
originalSense.example: If you don't clean your room, I'll have no choice but to ground you.

definition: To prevent an aircraft or pilot from flying.
example: The airline grounded the aircraft for additional inspections.
distinctions: Grounding prevents flight; landing brings an aircraft that is already flying back to the surface.
usage: Aviation.

originalSense.definition: To forbid (an aircraft or pilot) to fly.
originalSense.example: Because of the bad weather, all flights were grounded.

distinctionTask.prompt: After inspections found a fault, the airline _____ the aircraft so it could not fly.
distinctionTask.explanation: Grounded means prevented from flying; landed means brought an aircraft down from flight.

definition: To teach someone the basic principles of a subject.
example: The course grounds students in the principles of statistics.
distinctions: Grounding provides a foundation; specialist training develops more focused expertise.
usage: Usually ground someone in a subject.

originalSense.definition: To give a basic education in a particular subject; to instruct in elements or first principles.
originalSense.example: Jim was grounded in maths.

distinctionTask.prompt: The introductory course _____ students in the basic principles of statistics.
distinctionTask.explanation: Ground someone in a subject means teach its foundations; grind means crush or rub a material.

definition: To place a bat or part of the body on the ground behind a crease in cricket.
example: The batter grounded her bat behind the popping crease.
collocations: ground a foot behind the crease
distinctions: A grounded bat touches the ground; a bat merely held over the line may leave the batter out of her ground.
usage: Cricket; the applicable run-out or stumping law determines the decision.

originalSense.definition: To place a bat or part of the body on the ground to avoid being run out.

definition: To hit a ball that travels along or close to the ground.
example: The batter grounded to the shortstop.
distinctions: Ground describes a ground ball; fly describes a ball hit into the air. Ground out adds that the batter was put out.
usage: Baseball.

originalSense.definition: To hit a ground ball. Compare fly (verb (regular)) and line (verb).
originalSense.example: [Ichiro Suzuki] went 0 for 4, popping out in foul territory, grounding out to second, and striking out looking. And then, in the top of the eighth inning with a runner on second, the “True Hit King” grounded out to short, just barely failing to beat it out.

definition: To put something on the ground.
example: The porters grounded their packs beside the path.
distinctions: This ground means place on the surface; ground a circuit means make an electrical connection.
usage: Uncommon or formal transitive use; put down is more usual in everyday speech.

originalSense.definition: To place something on the ground.

definition: To strike the underwater bottom and become stuck.
example: The boat grounded on a sandbank at low tide.
distinctions: A vessel grounds when it strikes the bottom; it anchors when deliberately held by an anchor.
usage: Nautical; intransitive in this sense.

originalSense.definition: To run aground; to strike the bottom and remain fixed.
originalSense.example: The ship grounded on the bar.

definition: To base or establish something on a reason, principle or foundation.
example: The report grounds its conclusions in carefully documented evidence.
distinctions: Grounding supplies a basis for a claim; asserting a claim only states it.
usage: Often ground something in or on something.

originalSense.definition: To found; to fix or set, as on a foundation, reason, or principle; to furnish a ground for; to fix firmly.
originalSense.example: being rooted and grounded in love

definition: To prepare a surface with a coating or uniform background before further work.
example: The printmaker grounded the copper plate before drawing the design.
distinctions: Grounding prepares or coats the surface; etching removes exposed metal after the design is drawn.
usage: Fine arts and printmaking.

originalSense.definition: To cover with a ground, as a copper plate for etching, or as paper or other materials with a uniform tint as a preparation for ornament.

definition: To help someone feel mentally or emotionally steady and focused.
example: A short walk helps to ground her before a demanding meeting.
distinctions: Grounding concerns steadiness or connection to the present; distraction directs attention elsewhere.
usage: Figurative, often in descriptions of everyday emotional regulation.

originalSense.definition: To improve or focus the mental or emotional state of.
originalSense.example: I ground myself with meditation.

definition: To supply a model or its output with relevant external information as a basis for its response.
example: The retrieval system grounds the model’s answers in the supplied policy documents.
distinctions: Grounding provides relevant evidence or context; training changes model parameters. Supplying documents does not guarantee that every generated claim is correct.
usage: Machine learning and language-model applications.

originalSense.definition: To complement a machine learning model with relevant information it was not trained on.
originalSense.example: We design WikiChat (Figure 1) to ground LLMs using Wikipedia to achieve the following objectives. While LLMs tend to hallucinate, our chatbot should be factual.

definition: The past tense and past participle of grind.
example: She ground the coffee beans just before breakfast.
distinctions: Ground is the irregular past form of grind; grounded is the past form of the separate verb ground.
usage: Verb form: grind, ground, ground.

originalSense.definition: simple past and past participle of grind
originalSense.example: I ground the coffee up nicely.

distinctionTask.prompt: The irregular past tense of grind is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Grind, ground, ground is the irregular sequence. Grounded belongs to the separate verb ground.

definition: Crushed into small particles or powder.
example: Add a teaspoon of ground coriander to the sauce.
distinctions: Ground describes material reduced to particles; whole describes material kept unbroken.
usage: Adjective from grind; usually before a noun.

originalSense.definition: Crushed, or reduced to small particles.
originalSense.example: ground mustard seed

definition: Worked or finished by grinding.
example: The optical workshop used carefully ground lenses.
distinctions: Ground describes a grinding process; polished describes a smooth finish produced by polishing, which may be a later step.
usage: Manufacturing and optics. Ground glass can be roughened or frosted; a ground lens can be shaped by grinding and subsequently polished.

originalSense.definition: Processed by grinding.
originalSense.example: lenses of ground glass

definition: Relating to electricity or the electricity supply.
example: In some South Asian English varieties, a current bill is an electricity bill.
distinctions: Current here is a regional adjective meaning electrical; current costs in wider English usually means costs at the present time.
usage: South Asian English. The example explains the regional phrase; electricity bill is clearer for an international audience.

originalSense.definition: Electric; of or relating to electricity.
originalSense.example: current bill

definition: Running or moving swiftly.
example: In the older phrase “a creature that was current”, current describes a creature running or moving swiftly.
collocations: a creature that was current (obsolete source phrase)
distinctions: This obsolete adjective concerns movement; the modern current situation is the situation now.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the source quotation rather than offering a modern writing model.

originalSense.definition: Running or moving rapidly.
originalSense.example: For here we met, some ten or twelve of us, / To chase a creature that was current then / In these wild woods, the hart with golden horns.

definition: A family name.
example: Ms Current signed the attendance register.
distinctions: Capitalised Current can be a surname; lowercase current has separate ordinary noun and adjective meanings.
usage: Proper name. The example is illustrative and does not identify a real person.

originalSense.definition: A surname.

definition: Electricity or the electricity supply.
example: In South Asian English, “the current has gone” can mean that the electricity supply has failed.
collocations: the current has gone (South Asian English)
distinctions: This regional current can name the electricity supply as a whole; electric current in physics is the rate of charge flow.
usage: South Asian English. The example explains a regional expression; power outage is a widely understood description.

originalSense.definition: electricity, power in general.

distinctionTask.prompt: In South Asian English, “the current has gone” can describe a loss of the electricity _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This regional current names the electricity supply; it does not describe the price of electricity.

definition: An extra amount or effect beyond what was originally given, owed or experienced.
example: She returned his teasing with interest, making an even sharper joke.
distinctions: With interest can figuratively mean with something extra; financial interest is a charge or return associated with credit or invested money.
usage: Especially in the expression with interest; literal and figurative uses.

originalSense.definition: Any excess over and above an exact equivalent
originalSense.example: You shall have your desires with interest

distinctionTask.prompt: She returned his teasing with _____, making an even sharper joke.
distinctionTask.explanation: With interest can mean with something extra; principal is the original sum in a financial transaction.

definition: Injury or harm, or compensation paid for it.
example: In the older phrase “extreme interest and manifest derogation”, interest refers to harm or injury.
distinctions: This obsolete interest concerns injury or compensation; modern financial interest is distinct from damages.
usage: Obsolete and rare. The example explains the source’s wording; use harm, injury or damages in modern prose as appropriate.

originalSense.definition: Injury, or compensation for injury; damages.
originalSense.example: How can this infinite beauty, power and goodnes admit any correspondencie or similitude with a thing so base and abject as we are, without extreme interest and manifest derogation from his divine greatnesse?

definition: The people or businesses with a shared involvement in an industry, policy or cause, considered collectively.
example: Agricultural interests opposed the proposed import restrictions.
distinctions: Interests can mean the people or organisations concerned; an interest in a company can instead mean a stake held by one person or organisation.
usage: Often plural, especially when discussing business or political influence.

originalSense.definition: The persons and companies interested in any particular business or measure, taken collectively.
originalSense.example: the iron interest;  the cotton interest

distinctionTask.prompt: The phrase “agricultural interests opposed the policy” refers collectively to people and _____ connected with agriculture.
distinctionTask.explanation: Interests here names the people and businesses concerned, rather than their feelings of curiosity.

definition: A historical category of factual short films presenting varied subjects for general entertainment.
example: The historical programme listed an interest film about a little-known industry.
distinctions: An interest film was a broad historical film category; a modern documentary is a wider and differently organised category.
usage: Historical film terminology, usually attributive. It covered subjects not placed under labels such as fiction, travel or topical films.

originalSense.definition: A genre of factual short films, generally more amusing than informative, especially those not covered by a more specific genre label.
originalSense.example: By interest films is meant a variety of subjects which cannot be classified under such recognized headings as fiction, travel, or topical. They include wonderful inventions, little known industries, applied art, feats of engineering, and other events capable of effective illustration.

definition: To concern, involve or affect someone or something.
example: In the older clause “my cause doth interest this fair quarrel”, interest means concern or involve.
collocations: my cause doth interest this fair quarrel (obsolete source wording)
distinctions: This obsolete verb expresses involvement or concern; modern this topic interests me normally means it attracts my attention.
usage: Obsolete, sometimes impersonal. The example explains the source quotation.

originalSense.definition: To be concerned with or engaged in; to affect; to concern; to excite.
originalSense.example: Oh, rather, gracious sir, / Create me to this glory; since my cause / Doth interest this fair quarrel; valued least, / I am his equal.

definition: To cause or allow someone to share in something.
example: In the older phrase “interested in those precious blessings”, interested means made a participant in the blessings.
collocations: interest someone in something (obsolete sharing use)
distinctions: This older construction concerns participation or entitlement; modern interested in usually describes attention or curiosity.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the source’s religious wording; it is not a modern usage recommendation.

originalSense.definition: To cause or permit to share.
originalSense.example: The mystical communion of all faithful men is such as maketh every one to be interested in those precious blessings which any one of them receiveth at God's hands.

definition: The worth or value of something.
example: In the older expression “at such rate”, rate can refer to the value assigned to something.
distinctions: This obsolete noun names worth; a modern rate often expresses a quantity per unit or a set price.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the source construction rather than recommending it in modern prose.

originalSense.definition: The worth of something; value.
originalSense.example: There shall no figure at such rate be set, / As that of true and faithfull Iuliet.

definition: A class or rank, especially a historical classification of naval ships.
example: The naval register placed the ship in the third rate.
distinctions: A ship’s rate is its classification; its speed is how fast it travels. First-rate in ordinary modern English can mean excellent.
usage: Naval history. Criteria varied by navy and period; the British rating system often classified ships by their guns.

originalSense.definition: A class into which ships were assigned based on condition, size etc.; by extension, rank.
originalSense.example: This textbook is first-rate.

distinctionTask.prompt: In a historical naval register, a ship’s rate is its _____ rather than its speed.
distinctionTask.explanation: The naval rate is a class or rank; velocity describes motion.

definition: A fixed portion, allowance or ration.
example: In the older phrase “the evil rate of food”, rate means the poor allowance of food provided.
distinctions: This obsolete rate is an allotted portion; a rate of consumption measures how quickly a supply is used.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the source quotation.

originalSense.definition: Established portion or measure; fixed allowance; ration.
originalSense.example: The one right feeble through the evil rate / Of food which in her duress she had found.

definition: Order or arrangement.
example: In the older phrase “in seemly rate”, rate means an orderly arrangement.
distinctions: This obsolete noun concerns arrangement; rating in modern assessment concerns a score or rank.
usage: Obsolete and uncountable in this use. The example explains the source phrase.

originalSense.definition: Order; arrangement.
originalSense.example: Thus sat they all around in seemly rate.

definition: Ratification or approval.
example: In the older phrase “above the rate of Caesar”, rate refers to Caesar’s approval.
collocations: above the rate of Caesar (obsolete source wording)
distinctions: This obsolete noun means approval; a modern exchange rate expresses the relationship between two currencies.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the source quotation; approval is the usual modern word.

originalSense.definition: Ratification; approval.
originalSense.example:
c. 1610s, George Chapman, Caesar and Pompey
Tis offerd, Sir, 'boue the rate of Caesar
In other men, but in what I approue
Beneath his merits: which I will not faile
T'enforce at full to Pompey, nor forget
In any time the gratitude of my seruice.

definition: The amount by which a timepiece gains or loses time per unit of elapsed time.
example: The watch has a daily rate of plus two seconds: it gains two seconds each day.
collocations: a rate of plus two seconds per day
distinctions: Rate describes how the error changes over time; a watch being ten seconds fast describes its current offset.
usage: Horology. A positive rate denotes gaining time; a negative rate denotes losing time.

originalSense.definition: The gain or loss of a timepiece in a unit of time.
originalSense.example: daily rate; hourly rate; etc.

distinctionTask.prompt: A watch with a rate of +2 seconds per day _____ two seconds each day.
distinctionTask.explanation: A positive daily rate indicates gaining time. Its present offset is a separate measurement.

definition: To assess a property’s value for local taxation.
example: The valuation authority rated the premises for local taxation.
distinctions: Rating assesses the value used for taxation; collecting the tax is a separate action.
usage: Chiefly British English. The applicable valuation and tax system depends on the jurisdiction and period.

originalSense.definition: To evaluate a property's value for the purposes of local taxation.

definition: To restrain or control the pace of a horse during a race.
example: The jockey rated the horse through the first turn to conserve its energy.
distinctions: Rate here means control the horse’s pace; rate a horse’s chances means assess its prospects.
usage: Horse racing.

originalSense.definition: To take action to slow down the pace of the horse one is riding.
originalSense.example: Throughout the first turn is where the jockey rates the horse if the need arises. Rating a horse is where you keep it from putting out too much too soon.

definition: To hold a place in a particular class or ranking.
example: She rates among the most accomplished chefs in the region.
distinctions: Rate among describes a position in a group; rate someone highly describes another person’s favourable assessment.
usage: Intransitive.

originalSense.definition: To have position (in a certain class).
originalSense.example: She rates among the most excellent chefs in the world.

definition: To have a particular value, standing or level of approval.
example: The performance did not rate highly with the judges.
distinctions: Rate with the judges describes standing in their judgement; rate the judges makes the judges the objects being assessed.
usage: Intransitive.

originalSense.definition: To have value or standing.
originalSense.example: This last performance of hers didn't rate very high with the judges.

definition: To ratify or formally approve.
example: In the older phrase “to rate the truce”, rate means ratify the truce.
distinctions: This older rate means approve formally; modern rate a proposal usually means assess it.
usage: Rare or older use. The example explains the source construction; ratify is clearer in modern writing.

originalSense.definition: To ratify.
originalSense.example: to rate the truce

definition: To determine a chronometer’s gain or loss over time by comparison with a time reference.
example: The technician rated the chronometer against a reference clock over several days.
distinctions: Rating measures the gain or loss per unit time; setting a clock corrects its displayed time at one moment.
usage: Horology.

originalSense.definition: To ascertain the exact rate of the gain or loss of (a chronometer) as compared with true time.

distinctionTask.prompt: Rating a chronometer determines how much it gains or loses per unit of _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Chronometer rating compares timekeeping against a reference over time.

definition: To scold or rebuke someone.
example: In the older clause “then rated they him”, rated means scolded or rebuked.
distinctions: This obsolete rate means scold; modern rate someone normally means assess or rank them.
usage: Obsolete. The example modernises the pronoun in the source phrase for explanation.

originalSense.definition: To berate, scold.
originalSense.example: Then rated they hym, and sayde: Thou arte hys disciple.

definition: To cause plant material to decay through exposure to weather or moisture, sometimes as part of retting.
example: In the historical flax account, the stems were spread on the rating ground until sufficiently rated.
distinctions: Rating can refer to controlled retting that separates fibres, or unwanted decay; grading assesses quality without causing decay.
usage: Obsolete British dialect. The example paraphrases the source’s flax-processing account rather than giving processing instructions.

originalSense.definition: To cause (hay, hemp, flax, etc) to decay (whether in an injurious way, or—as retting—in a useful way) by exposure to weather, particularly wetness.
originalSense.example: From the "line pit" it [flax] is carried to the “RATING GROUND;" - a piece of unbroken aftergrass, where the sheaflets are untied, and the flax spread thin upon the grass. It is calculated, that a full crop ought to cover as much ground as it grew upon. Here it lies until it be sufficiently "rated;" namely, until the more woodlike substance of the stems will separate […]

definition: Knowledge, skills or cultural familiarity treated as a useful resource.
example: Interpreters draw on cultural capital as well as knowledge of vocabulary.
distinctions: Cultural capital concerns socially useful cultural resources; financial capital concerns money or financial assets.
usage: Often in combinations such as cultural capital. The term can cover more than factual knowledge alone.

originalSense.definition: Knowledge; awareness; proficiency.
originalSense.example: Interpreters need a good amount of cultural capital in order to function efficiently in the profession.

distinctionTask.prompt: In “cultural capital”, capital can include useful cultural knowledge and _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Cultural capital concerns cultural resources; banknotes are money.

definition: The chief or most important thing.
example: In this uncommon noun sense, capital names the chief or most important thing under discussion.
collocations: capital meaning the principal thing (uncommon noun)
distinctions: This noun names the principal thing; capital as an adjective can describe something of prime importance.
usage: Uncommon extended noun sense. The example is a reading explanation of the recorded definition, not an attested quotation.

originalSense.definition: The chief or most important thing.

definition: Excellent or very good.
example: That is a capital idea; let us try it.
distinctions: Capital here praises quality; a capital city is a seat of government.
usage: Dated, especially British English. It can sound deliberately old-fashioned today.

originalSense.definition: Excellent.
originalSense.example: a capital fellow

definition: Relating to the head.
example: Milton’s phrase “his capital bruise” refers to a wound to the head.
distinctions: Capital here refers to the head; capital punishment refers to the death penalty.
usage: Rare, chiefly historical anatomical or literary use. The example explains the source phrase.

originalSense.definition: Of or relating to the head.
originalSense.example: Needs must the Serpent now his capital bruise / Expect with mortal pain.

definition: An exclamation expressing approval or delight.
example: “We have secured the room.” “Capital!”
distinctions: Capital! is an approving exclamation; capital letters are uppercase characters.
usage: Dated informal exclamation, especially British English.

originalSense.definition: used as an expression of approval, satisfaction, or delight.
originalSense.example: That's an amazing idea! Capital!

definition: The former US airline Capital Airlines, which merged with United Airlines in 1961.
example: The aviation history describes Capital’s merger with United in 1961.
distinctions: Capital here is the airline’s proper name; lowercase capital can mean funds, a government city or other ordinary senses.
usage: Historical proper name. This refers to the former US carrier, not another airline with a similar name.

originalSense.definition: The Capital Airlines, which operated as a trunk carrier in the United States before merging with United Airlines in 1961.
originalSense.example: Fornasero had been a pilot for almost 19 years and joined Capital in 1941. He spent three years as a pilot for the Air Force during World War II and then rejoined the airline.

definition: Capital Governorate, an administrative region of Bahrain.
example: The report lists Manama within Bahrain’s Capital Governorate.
distinctions: Capital Governorate is an administrative region; Manama is the city that serves as Bahrain’s capital.
usage: Proper name. Include Bahrain to distinguish it from similarly named administrative regions elsewhere.

originalSense.definition: A governorate in northern Bahrain.

definition: Used with a named capital letter to emphasise that a description applies strongly or completely.
example: The sudden silence meant Trouble with a capital T.
distinctions: The named uppercase letter adds emphasis to the description; it does not change the ordinary spelling of every occurrence of the word.
usage: Usually in the construction with a capital followed by the word’s initial letter.

originalSense.definition: Used to emphasise greatness or absoluteness.

distinctionTask.prompt: “Trouble with a capital T” uses the capital letter to add _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The named initial adds emphasis to the description; it does not describe financial capital.

definition: The person or organisation acting as banker or controlling the stakes in a card game.
example: The rules allow a different player to act as the bank in each round.
distinctions: The bank here is the role or party controlling the game’s stakes; the bank can separately mean the fund used to pay losses.
usage: Card games and gambling.

originalSense.definition: An underwriter or controller of a card game.

definition: A pooled fund of contributions used for a business or shared enterprise.
example: The partners contributed to a common bank of capital for the venture.
distinctions: This bank is the pooled fund; a financial bank is the institution that may hold the money.
usage: Uncommon or older financial use.

originalSense.definition: A fund from deposits or contributions, to be used in transacting business; a joint stock or capital.
originalSense.example: Let it be no bank or common stock, but every man be master of his own money.

definition: The fund used by a dealer or banker to take stakes and pay winnings in a game.
example: The dealer paid the winning player from the bank.
distinctions: The bank is the available fund; the banker is the person or party managing it.
usage: Gambling terminology.

originalSense.definition: The sum of money etc. which the dealer or banker has as a fund from which to draw stakes and pay losses.

definition: Money or profit.
example: She made good bank from the successful tour.
distinctions: Bank here means money or profit; a bank account is a record held by a financial institution.
usage: Slang, especially in expressions such as make bank. Avoid it in formal academic prose.

originalSense.definition: Money; profit.
originalSense.example: Military dude was working for a drug dealer, right? and making good bank with it—he was making good money.

definition: The reserve of pieces from which players draw in a game such as dominoes.
example: When she could not play, she drew another domino from the bank.
distinctions: The bank holds unclaimed pieces; a player’s hand contains the pieces already held by that player.
usage: Board and tile games. Rules vary by game.

originalSense.definition: In certain games, such as dominos, a fund of pieces from which the players are allowed to draw.

definition: A stored group of instrument sounds or preset data on a digital synthesizer.
example: The synthesizer stores the drum kits in bank 1.
distinctions: A bank groups stored sounds or presets; a preset is an individual saved configuration or sound.
usage: Electronic music. Exact bank and preset organisation depends on the instrument.

originalSense.definition: A collection of instrument data on a digital synthesizer.
originalSense.example: All of the drum kits are on bank 1.

distinctionTask.prompt: On this synthesizer, a preset bank groups several saved _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The electronic-music bank contains sound or instrument data.

definition: To conceal something in the rectum, especially contraband in prison.
example: The prison glossary labels bank as slang for concealing contraband in the rectum.
distinctions: This prison slang concerns concealment; bank money in ordinary English means deposit it with a financial institution.
usage: Prison slang. The example explains the recorded meaning without describing a method.

originalSense.definition: To conceal in the rectum for use in prison.
originalSense.example: Johnny banked some coke for me.

definition: To provide banking services to a person or organisation.
example: The initiative aims to bank people in remote communities who lack financial services.
distinctions: Bank is transitive here: the institution banks its clients. Bank with an institution describes the customer’s relationship instead.
usage: Finance and financial-inclusion discussions.

originalSense.definition: To provide banking services to.
originalSense.example: They proposed an ambitious plan to bank people in remote rural communities.

distinctionTask.prompt: A scheme to bank underserved communities aims to provide financial _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This transitive bank means provide banking services.

definition: A slope or hill, especially an incline on a railway.
example: The freight train climbed the long bank beyond the junction.
distinctions: A bank is an incline in this use; a bank beside a river is land at the water’s edge.
usage: Especially railway terminology.

originalSense.definition: An incline, a hill.
originalSense.example: This is the hardest duty on the railway, for the trains are heavy and there are some long 1 in 40 banks.

definition: The exposed face of coal where miners are working.
example: The mining report describes workers cutting coal at the bank.
distinctions: This bank is the working face of the coal; another mining sense names the surface at the top of a shaft.
usage: Specialist mining terminology.

originalSense.definition: The face of the coal at which miners are working.

definition: A deposit of ore or coal worked by excavations above water level.
example: The historical mine survey lists an ore bank worked above water level.
distinctions: The bank is the mineral deposit being worked; the shaft is an access opening.
usage: Specialist mining use. The above-water-level qualification belongs to this recorded definition.

originalSense.definition: A deposit of ore or coal, worked by excavations above water level.

definition: The surface ground at the top of a mine shaft.
example: The ore was brought to bank and loaded into wagons.
distinctions: Bank here is the surface at the shaft top; the working face is where material is extracted underground.
usage: Mining terminology, often in older accounts.

originalSense.definition: The ground at the top of a shaft.
originalSense.example: Ores are brought to bank.

definition: To tilt an aircraft so that one wing is lower than the other.
example: The pilot banked the aircraft to the left during the turn.
collocations: bank a plane to the left
distinctions: Banking is rotation about the aircraft’s longitudinal axis; pitching raises or lowers the nose.
usage: Aviation; transitive. A coordinated turn involves more than tilting the aircraft alone.

originalSense.definition: To cause (an aircraft) to bank.

definition: To pile material into a raised heap or ridge.
example: The workers banked the earth along the edge of the path.
distinctions: Banking piles material into a ridge; spreading distributes it over an area.
usage: Transitive, often bank up.

originalSense.definition: To form into a bank or heap, to bank up.
originalSense.example: to bank sand

definition: To gather into a thick mass, especially of clouds.
example: Dark clouds banked above the hills before the storm.
distinctions: Banking describes clouds gathering in a mass; dispersing describes them spreading out or breaking up.
usage: Intransitive, chiefly of clouds.

originalSense.definition: To form a bank; to gather in masses.
originalSense.example: […] clouds banking above the gravel road, their flat slate-blue bottoms threatening freezing rain or an early snowfall.

definition: To cover or arrange a fire’s embers so that they retain heat and burn slowly.
example: The novel describes the hearth fire as banked for the night.
distinctions: A banked fire retains heat and may still contain live embers; an extinguished fire has been put out.
usage: Traditional fire-management term. The example describes a literary scene rather than giving fire-handling instructions.

originalSense.definition: To cover the embers of a fire with ashes in order to retain heat.

definition: To enclose or protect something with a raised mound or embankment.
example: The river was banked to protect the adjoining fields.
distinctions: Banking creates an embankment; dredging removes material from a waterway’s bed.
usage: Transitive; embank is often clearer in modern technical writing.

originalSense.definition: To raise a mound or dike about; to enclose, defend, or fortify with a bank; to embank.
originalSense.example: Aristoma∣chus would haue them to be stript from their leaues in winter, & in any hand to be banked well about, that the water stand not there in any hollow furrow or hole lower than the other ground

definition: To travel past the banks or waterside of a place.
example: In the older phrase “as I have banked their towns”, banked means passed their towns along the waterside.
distinctions: This obsolete verb concerns travelling past a waterside place; modern bank with a company concerns financial services.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the source quotation rather than inventing a modern use.

originalSense.definition: To pass by the banks of.
originalSense.example: Have I not heard these islanders shout out / Vive le roi! as I have banked their towns?

definition: To assist a train on an incline with an additional locomotive.
example: An extra locomotive banked the heavy freight train up the incline.
distinctions: A banking engine adds traction on an incline; a brake reduces or controls the train’s speed.
usage: British railway terminology. The assisting engine is often at the rear.

originalSense.definition: To provide additional power for a train ascending a bank (incline) by attaching another locomotive.
originalSense.example: Some interesting facts have recently been made known by the L.N.E.R. concerning the 178-ton Garratt 2-8-0 + 0-8-2 engine No. 2395, which since construction in 1925 has spent the whole of its working life banking coal trains up the 3 miles of 1 in 40 between Wentworth junction and West Silkstone, on the Worsborough branch, near Barnsley.

distinctionTask.prompt: A banking engine helps a heavy train climb an _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: In British railway terminology, banking provides extra locomotive power on an incline.

definition: A row or set of keys on a musical keyboard or typewriter.
example: The organist moved from the lower bank of keys to the upper one.
distinctions: A bank groups keys in a row or tier; one key is an individual control.
usage: Keyboard instruments and older keyboard descriptions.

originalSense.definition: A row of keys on a musical keyboard or the equivalent on a typewriter keyboard.

definition: A hardware-defined group or block of memory that can be selected or accessed as a unit.
example: The controller selected a different memory bank before reading the next block of data.
distinctions: A bank is a hardware-defined memory grouping; a page is another memory unit whose size and relation to banks depend on the system.
usage: Computing. In bank-switched systems a bank can be a contiguous block; other hardware may interleave addresses across banks. Bank size and its relation to pages are not universal.

originalSense.definition: A contiguous block of memory that is of fixed, hardware-dependent size, but often larger than a page and partitioning the memory such that two distinct banks do not overlap.

definition: A group of adjacent drop targets on a pinball machine.
example: The ball knocked down the last target in the bank.
distinctions: The bank is the group of targets; a drop target is one target that lowers when hit.
usage: Pinball.

originalSense.definition: A set of multiple adjacent drop targets.

definition: To arrange things together in a row or tier.
example: The consoles were banked along the wall of the control room.
distinctions: Bank here concerns arrangement; bank money concerns depositing it.
usage: Transitive; often passive.

originalSense.definition: To arrange or order in a row.

definition: A bench for rowers, or a tier of oars on a rowing vessel.
example: The historical account places the rowers on banks along the galley.
distinctions: A bank can be the rowers’ bench or an oar tier; an oar is the implement used for rowing.
usage: Historical nautical terminology.

originalSense.definition: A bench, as for rowers in a galley; also, a tier of oars.
originalSense.example: Placed on their banks, the lusty Trojans sweep / Neptune's smooth face, and cleave the yielding deep.

definition: A bench or seat occupied by judges in a court.
example: The legal glossary records bank as an older name for the judges’ bench.
distinctions: Bank here names the judges’ seat; another legal sense concerns the court sitting as a body.
usage: Older legal terminology. The example is an explicit reading explanation; bench is the usual modern English word.

originalSense.definition: A bench or seat for judges in court.

definition: A regular court term or a full court sitting to hear questions of law.
example: In the older expression “in bank”, the court sits to hear questions of law.
distinctions: This legal bank concerns the court’s sitting, contrasted in older usage with nisi prius proceedings; en banc is the related modern expression.
usage: Historical legal terminology. Court structures and the meaning of en banc vary by jurisdiction.

originalSense.definition: The regular term of a court of law, or the full court sitting to hear arguments upon questions of law, as distinguished from a sitting at nisi prius, or a court held for jury trials. See banc

definition: A table used by printers.
example: The printing-history glossary identifies a bank as a printer’s table.
distinctions: This archaic bank is a table used in printing; a financial bank is an institution.
usage: Archaic printing terminology. The example explains the recorded definition without inventing a specific table design or use.

originalSense.definition: A kind of table used by printers.

definition: A bench or row of keys associated with a keyboard instrument, such as an organ.
example: The historical music glossary gives bank as either a bench or a row of organ keys.
distinctions: This source groups a bench and a keyboard row under bank; in modern writing, organ bench and manual distinguish those objects clearly.
usage: Specialist or historical music terminology. The example is a reading explanation of the source’s combined definition.

originalSense.definition: A bench, or row of keys belonging to a keyboard, as in an organ.

definition: A village in the New Forest, Hampshire, England.
example: The walking guide marks Bank in the New Forest.
distinctions: Capitalised Bank is the village name here; lowercase bank has separate financial and geographical meanings.
usage: Proper name. Include Hampshire or New Forest to identify the location.

originalSense.definition: A village in the New Forest in Hampshire, England.

definition: A London Underground station in the City of London, named after the Bank of England.
example: The journey planner suggests changing trains at Bank.
distinctions: Bank is a station name here; the Bank of England is the institution from which the station takes its name.
usage: Proper name, normally capitalised.

originalSense.definition: A major London Underground station in the City of London, named after the Bank of England and one of the busiest stations on the network (OS grid ref TQ3281)
originalSense.example: Anybody familiar with the London Underground network will know that Bank Tube station is a place to be avoided - if at all possible - on a weekday morning. Located at the very heart of London's 'Square Mile' financial district, some 70,000 people detrain there during the morning peak, to pass through its gatelines and those at the adjoining station at Monument. A further 50,000 passengers squeeze into the station complex at exactly the same time of day, in order to change between the five lines that pass through it.

definition: A family name.
example: Dr Bank presented the opening lecture.
distinctions: Capitalised Bank can be a surname; lowercase bank names several unrelated ordinary meanings.
usage: Proper name. The example is illustrative and makes no claim about a particular person.

originalSense.definition: A surname.

definition: A load or burden carried by a person, vehicle or vessel.
example: The historical account describes a ship carrying a charge of cargo and passengers.
distinctions: Charge is the load being carried; an electrical charge is a property of matter.
usage: Often literary or older in the general cargo sense; load or cargo is more usual today.

originalSense.definition: A load or burden; cargo.
originalSense.example: The ship had a charge of colonists and their belongings.

definition: An instruction or command assigning a task.
example: The committee received a charge to review the policy before June.
distinctions: A charge directs someone to act; a charge against someone is an accusation.
usage: Often formal.

originalSense.definition: An instruction.
originalSense.example: I gave him the charge to get the deal closed by the end of the month.

definition: A legal security interest over property used to secure a debt or obligation.
example: The lender registered a charge over the property.
distinctions: A property charge secures an obligation; a service charge is a fee. A mortgage is one form or closely related arrangement, depending on local law.
usage: Property law. Exact rights, terminology and registration rules depend on the jurisdiction.

originalSense.definition: A mortgage.

distinctionTask.prompt: A legal charge over property can provide _____ for a debt.
distinctionTask.explanation: A property charge secures an obligation; it is unrelated to a criminal finding of guilt.

definition: An offensive foul involving illegal contact by a player with the ball against a defender in a legal guarding position.
example: The referee called a charge when the ball-handler ran into the legally positioned defender.
distinctions: A charge is an offensive foul; blocking is a defensive foul. A defender need not be completely motionless in every situation.
usage: Basketball. Legal guarding position and restricted-area rules depend on the competition; a stationary defender alone does not define every charge.

originalSense.definition: An offensive foul in which the player with the ball moves into a stationary defender.

definition: A measured amount of powder or shot in a firearm cartridge.
example: The museum label describes the cartridge’s powder charge.
distinctions: Charge names the measured contents in this use; cartridge names the complete ammunition unit.
usage: Firearms terminology. The example identifies a historical display without describing preparation or use.

originalSense.definition: A measured amount of powder and/or shot in a cartridge.

definition: A measured quantity of explosive material.
example: The safety report records that the explosive charge was removed by specialists.
distinctions: A charge is a quantity of explosive; an explosion is the event that may result from its detonation.
usage: Explosives terminology. The example is descriptive and gives no operating instructions.

originalSense.definition: A measured amount of explosive.
originalSense.example: Watt might have broken the door down, with an axe, or a crow, or a small charge of explosive, but this might have aroused Erskine's suspicions, and Watt did not want that.

definition: An emblem or figure displayed on a heraldic shield.
example: The shield bears a lion as its central charge.
distinctions: The charge is the emblem or figure; the field is the shield’s background.
usage: Heraldry.

originalSense.definition: An image displayed on an escutcheon.
originalSense.example: Near-synonym: emblem

distinctionTask.prompt: In heraldry, the emblem on a shield is the charge; the background is the _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The heraldic field is the background bearing the charge.

definition: A position in which a weapon is held ready for an attack.
example: The historical drill manual uses “to the charge” for an attacking weapon position.
collocations: bring a weapon to the charge
distinctions: The charge here is a weapon position; a military charge is an attack involving forward movement.
usage: Historical weaponry and drill terminology. The example explains a phrase without giving drill instructions.

originalSense.definition: A position (of a weapon) fitted for attack.
originalSense.example: to bring a weapon to the charge

definition: A plaster or ointment used in traditional horse care.
example: The farriery glossary records charge as a kind of plaster or ointment.
collocations: a charge meaning a plaster (traditional farriery)
distinctions: This specialist charge is an applied preparation; a service charge is a fee.
usage: Traditional farriery. The example explains a historical material name and makes no claim about effectiveness or modern treatment.

originalSense.definition: A sort of plaster or ointment.

definition: Importance, significance or value.
example: In the older phrase “of great charge”, charge can mean importance or weight.
distinctions: Charge here means significance; a modern charge often means a fee or accusation.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the source’s expression rather than recommending it in modern prose.

originalSense.definition: Weight; import; value.
originalSense.example: many suchlike as's of great charge

definition: A historical measure of lead comprising thirty-six pigs, each described as weighing about seventy pounds.
example: The historical trade record gives the quantity of lead in charges.
distinctions: A charge is a bulk measure here; a pig of lead is one cast ingot within it.
usage: Historical or obsolete unit. The source’s approximate ingot weight should not be treated as a universal modern standard.

originalSense.definition: A measure of thirty-six pigs of lead, each pig weighing about seventy pounds; a charre.

definition: A formal address delivered at a church service concluding a visitation.
example: The bishop delivered a charge at the close of the visitation.

originalSense.definition: An address given at a church service concluding a visitation.

definition: Cannabis.

originalSense.definition: To impute or ascribe.

definition: To place a burden, load or responsibility on someone or something.

definition: To fill equipment with the material needed for its operation.

usage: Technical transitive use. The example names an operation without giving handling instructions.

originalSense.definition: To load equipment with material required for its use, as a firearm with powder, a fire hose with water, a chemical reactor with raw materials.
originalSense.example: Charge your weapons; we're moving up.

definition: To lie flat and remain still, as directed by a command to a hunting dog.

distinctions: This command directs the dog to remain still; charge in ordinary movement contexts means rush forwards.

originalSense.definition: To lie on the belly and be still. (A command given by a hunter to a dog)

definition: Short for CHARGE syndrome, the name of a congenital medical syndrome.

originalSense.definition: Ellipsis of CHARGE syndrome.

definition: A formal allegation by police or a court that someone has committed a crime.

usage: Criminal law. Procedures and terminology vary by jurisdiction.

originalSense.definition: An official description (by the police or a court) of a crime that somebody may be guilty of.

distinctionTask.prompt: A criminal charge is an allegation, while a finding of guilt can result in a _____.

definition: An accusation made by a person or organisation.
example: The editor rejected the charge that the article was biased.

usage: General and formal use; a legal prosecution is not implied.

originalSense.definition: An accusation by a person or organization.

definition: To decorate something with an emblem or cause it to bear one.

originalSense.definition: To cause to take on an electric charge.

originalSense.definition: To replenish energy to (a battery, or a device containing a battery) by use of an electrical device plugged into a power outlet.

distinctionTask.prompt: Charging a phone battery replenishes its stored _____.

distinctions: The battery charges is intransitive; she charges the battery is transitive. Both describe replenishing stored energy.
usage: Intransitive, of a rechargeable battery or a device containing one.

originalSense.definition: To replenish energy.

definition: To attack by rushing forwards, especially as a group.

usage: Military or historical narrative; transitive or intransitive according to the construction.

originalSense.definition: To attack by moving forward quickly in a group.

originalSense.definition: To commit a charging foul.

example: The service account is the principal whose identity the system authenticates.
