usage: Transitive verb, often used in academic writing.

originalSense.definition: To make clear to one's mind or intelligence; to put forward for consideration.
originalSense.example: I do begin to realize that the matter must be presented in such a way as may interest the reader.

distinctionTask.prompt: Presenting results concerns how they are _____; producing results concerns obtaining them.
distinctionTask.explanation: Presentation communicates information without itself proving it true.

definition: To stage or put on a performance or production.
example: The college will present a new play next month.
distinctions: Present a play means put it on for an audience; compose or write a play concerns creating the text.
usage: Transitive verb in performance announcements.

originalSense.definition: To put on, stage (a play etc.).

definition: To point or hold a firearm in a position ready for use.

definition: To occur to the mind or become available for consideration.

originalSense.definition: To offer oneself for mental consideration; to occur to the mind.
originalSense.example: Well, one idea does present itself.

definition: To offer or convey something abstract, such as thanks or compliments.

definition: To hand over a bill or similar document for payment.

definition: In some animals, to adopt a sexually receptive posture displaying the genital region.

definition: To court someone or make a romantic approach.

definition: To turn one’s attention or efforts to something.

distinctions: A project in this sports sense is a developing player; it does not guarantee future success.
usage: US sports terminology; noun. The example is illustrative.

originalSense.definition: A raw recruit who the team hopes will improve greatly with coaching; a long shot, diamond in the rough.
originalSense.example: Sakho was seen as no-frills, whereas Maiga was a project who could develop into the next big thing.

definition: To stick out beyond a surface or edge.
example: The balcony projects beyond the front wall.
distinctions: This intransitive project means protrude; project an image is a transitive use involving a displayed image.
usage: Verb: second-syllable stress, proJECT.

originalSense.definition: To extend beyond a surface.

distinctionTask.prompt: A balcony that projects beyond a wall _____ beyond it.
distinctionTask.explanation: Project has a spatial protrusion sense as well as an estimation sense.

definition: To cast an image, shadow or other visible form onto a surface.
example: The device projected the diagram onto the screen.
distinctions: Projecting an image displays it on a surface; projecting a future total estimates it.
usage: Transitive verb, with onto often introducing the receiving surface.

originalSense.definition: To cast (an image or shadow) upon a surface; to throw or cast forward; to shoot forth.
originalSense.example: Before his feet her selfe she did proiect

definition: To extend a part or appendage outwards.
example: The snail projected its tentacles beyond the shell.
distinctions: This transitive project states the part extended as its object; the balcony projects uses the intransitive construction.
usage: Transitive verb with second-syllable stress.

originalSense.definition: To extend (a protrusion or appendage) outward.

definition: To plan for or estimate a future state or result.
example: The model projects an increase from 100 to 120 units next year.
distinctions: A projection depends on assumptions and available data; it is not a guarantee. In the example, 100 to 120 is a 20-unit or 20% increase.
usage: Transitive verb with second-syllable stress. State the assumptions when they matter.

originalSense.definition: To make plans for; to forecast.
originalSense.example: The CEO is projecting the completion of the acquisition by April 2007.

distinctionTask.prompt: A projected change from 100 to 120 is a _____ increase, assuming the projection occurs.
distinctionTask.explanation: The increase is 20 relative to the starting 100, giving 20%. A projection is conditional on its assumptions.

definition: To convey a particular impression or image of oneself.
example: She projected confidence during the presentation.
distinctions: Project confidence concerns the impression conveyed; it does not establish how confident someone feels internally.
usage: Transitive or reflexive use; second-syllable stress.

originalSense.definition: To present (oneself), to convey a certain impression, usually in a good way.
originalSense.example: It is difficult to gauge the exact point at which women stop trying to fool men and really begin to deceive themselves, but an objective analyst cannot escape the conclusion (1) that partly from a natural device inherent in the species, women deliberately project upon actual or potential suitors an impression of themselves that is not an accurate picture of their total nature, and (2) that few women ever are privileged to see themselves as they really are.

distinctionTask.prompt: Projecting confidence describes the _____ someone conveys.
distinctionTask.explanation: The impression conveyed need not match the person’s internal feeling.

definition: To attribute one’s own feelings or attitudes to someone else.
example: In the fictional example, he projects his own anxiety onto his colleague.
distinctions: Projection attributes one’s own state to someone else; it is not evidence of that other person’s feelings. A single action does not establish a clinical diagnosis.
usage: Psychology or psychoanalytic terminology; the example explains the concept.

originalSense.definition: To assume qualities or mindsets in others based on one's own personality.

definition: To transform spatial coordinates into another map projection or coordinate reference system.
example: The analyst projected the data from geographic coordinates into a suitable local projected coordinate system.
distinctions: Reprojection changes coordinate values to represent locations in another system; assigning a coordinate system labels how existing numbers are interpreted. A change of datum may require an additional transformation.
usage: Cartography and GIS. Projection can change scale, shape, area or other map properties.

originalSense.definition: To change the projection (or coordinate system) of spatial data with another projection.

distinctionTask.prompt: Reprojecting spatial data changes coordinates; assigning a CRS mainly changes their _____.
options: measured location by physically moving the feature
distinctionTask.explanation: Assigning a CRS labels how existing values are interpreted. Reprojection calculates values in another CRS.

definition: To form a new geometric figure by drawing rays from a fixed point through the original figure to a receiving surface.
example: In the construction, points A and B are projected from centre P onto the target line.
distinctions: This central projection uses rays through a fixed centre; parallel projection instead uses parallel projecting lines.
usage: Geometry. The diagram is a two-dimensional cross-section of the construction.

originalSense.definition: To draw straight lines from a fixed point through every point of any body or figure, and let these fall upon a surface so as to form the points of a new figure.

distinctionTask.prompt: Central projection uses rays through _____; parallel projection uses parallel lines.
distinctionTask.explanation: The illustrated central construction uses the same finite centre P for each ray.

definition: For neurons, to extend axons to another region.
example: Neurons in this region project to the spinal cord.
distinctions: A neural projection describes anatomical connections; it does not alone specify every effect or the direction of all information flow through a circuit.
usage: Neuroanatomy; the example illustrates a connection without describing a particular clinical condition.

originalSense.definition: (of a neuron or group of neurons) to have axon(s) extending to and therefore able to influence a remote location

definition: To make one’s voice or words carry to listeners at a distance.
example: The actor projected her voice to the back of the hall.
collocations: project to the back of a room
distinctions: Projecting a voice concerns making it carry clearly; it need not mean shouting.
usage: Transitive verb, common in performance contexts.

originalSense.definition: To cause (one's voice or words) to be heard at a great distance.
originalSense.example: to project one's voice

definition: To speak or sing so that one can be heard at a distance.
example: Even without a microphone, the speaker could project well.
distinctions: This intransitive project has no direct object; project one’s voice names the voice as its object.
usage: Intransitive verb with second-syllable stress.

originalSense.definition: To speak or sing in such a way that one can be heard at a great distance.
originalSense.example: You would think that topic coulda put me to sleep, but HE can really project when HE wants to.

definition: To extend an idea, inference or interpretation to another point or context.
example: The historian warned against projecting modern assumptions back into the past.
distinctions: Projecting an assumption into another period extends an interpretation; it does not establish that people in that period held the assumption.
usage: Figurative transitive use.

originalSense.definition: To extend to reach a point.
originalSense.example: When a word occurs only in Indo-European languages of northern or western Europe, for instance, projecting that word back to Proto-Indo-European is considered dubious.

definition: To make or yield something, without stating it as a direct object.
example: The factory continued to produce throughout the year.
distinctions: This intransitive construction leaves the product unstated; produce containers gives the transitive verb a direct object.
usage: Intransitive verb with second-syllable stress.

originalSense.definition: To make or yield something.
originalSense.example: Now it is also my understanding, I believe I am correct in this, that either one or two other manufacturers did not produce this year, which also created a certain shortage.

definition: To bring forward or make something available for inspection or use.
example: She produced her ticket when the inspector asked to see it.
distinctions: Produce a ticket makes an existing ticket available; it does not normally mean manufacture the ticket in that context.
usage: Transitive verb with second-syllable stress.

originalSense.definition: To make (a thing) available to a person, an authority, etc.; to provide for inspection.
originalSense.example: It was necessary for the prisoner to produce a witness to prove his innocency.

distinctionTask.prompt: Producing a ticket for an inspector normally means _____ it.
distinctionTask.explanation: The inspection sense makes an existing item available.

definition: To organise, finance or oversee the making of a film, programme or other production.
example: The company produced a documentary about urban gardens.
distinctions: Producing a film concerns arranging or overseeing its making; directing guides its creative realisation. Responsibilities vary and one person may hold both roles.
usage: Media production; transitive verb.

originalSense.definition: To sponsor and present (a motion picture, etc) to an audience or to the public.
originalSense.example: David Tickle flew in to Melbourne to produce the quad-platinum (in Australia) LP “True Colors” and the triple gold single “I Got You”— both of which shot the band to international prominence.

definition: To extend a line segment or side beyond an endpoint along the same straight line.
example: Produce side AB beyond B to a new point C.
collocations: produce a side of a triangle
distinctions: Produce AB beyond B extends the line through B; it does not create a second parallel segment.
usage: Geometry; formal instruction wording. The diagram uses collinear points A, B and C.

originalSense.definition: To extend an area, or lengthen a line.
originalSense.example: to produce a side of a triangle

distinctionTask.prompt: Produce AB beyond B to C means A, B and C lie on _____ line.
distinctionTask.explanation: The geometric instruction extends the side through B to C.

definition: To prolong or extend something in time or extent.
example: In the older phrase “produce a mans life”, produce means prolong the person’s life.
collocations: produce a mans life (obsolete source wording)
distinctions: This obsolete produce means prolong; modern produce a result normally means cause or generate it.
usage: Obsolete. The note explains the recorded wording and makes no claim about how to prolong life.

originalSense.definition: To draw out; to extend; to lengthen or prolong.
originalSense.example: And truely there goes a great deale of providence to produce a mans life unto threeſcore; […]

definition: To shape a musical recording using production techniques or technology.
example: The producer carefully produced the track’s layered electronic sound.
distinctions: Production shapes a recording’s sound; performance supplies the musical playing or singing. A recording can involve both.
usage: Music; this sense focuses on the recording’s treatment rather than only sponsorship or release.

originalSense.definition: To alter using technology, as opposed to simply performing.
originalSense.example: highly produced sound

definition: What is made, yielded or generated.
example: The sale displayed the produce of local workshops.
distinctions: Produce can broadly name what is yielded; in everyday shopping contexts it more often means fresh farm food.
usage: Usually uncountable; first-syllable stress: PROduce. This broad product sense can sound formal or older.

originalSense.definition: That which is produced.

definition: Farm or garden food products collectively, especially fruit and vegetables.
example: The market sells fresh local produce.
distinctions: Produce is normally uncountable: use some produce, not several produces. The scope can be wider than fruit and vegetables in some contexts.
usage: Noun with first-syllable stress. Context may include other farm products.

originalSense.definition: Harvested agricultural goods collectively, especially vegetables and fruit, but possibly including eggs, dairy products and meat; the saleable food products of farms.
originalSense.example: All fruits, vegetables, and dairy and poultry-yard produce are, in the Australian capitals, dear, and of very easy sale.

distinctionTask.prompt: A natural collective phrase for fresh fruit and vegetables is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The farm-food noun produce is normally uncountable and has first-syllable stress.

definition: The offspring of an animal, especially in breeding terminology.
example: The breeder recorded the mare’s produce for that season.
distinctions: Produce names offspring here; farm produce in a shop usually names food products. The animals’ actual relationships depend on the breeding record.
usage: Animal-breeding terminology; noun with first-syllable stress.

originalSense.definition: Offspring.
originalSense.example: With regard to the mare that has proved herself of the first class during her racing career, let us contrast the probable success of her produce […]

definition: Livestock feed and pet food supplies.
example: The Australian produce store sells feed for horses and poultry.
distinctions: In this Australian retail use, produce can concern animal feed; a produce section in a supermarket usually concerns fruit and vegetables.
usage: Australian usage; noun with first-syllable stress.

originalSense.definition: Livestock and pet food supplies.

definition: Rejected or discarded as unwanted or unsuitable.
example: The refuse material was set aside for recycling.
distinctions: The adjective describes material that has been rejected; the noun refuse collectively names waste. Neither uses the final voiced sound of the refusal verb.
usage: Adjective, often attributive or older. Like the waste noun, it normally has first-syllable stress and final /s/.

originalSense.definition: Discarded, rejected.

definition: To decline or reject a request, offer or demand.
example: She refused the offer politely.
distinctions: Refuse an offer rejects it; deny an allegation says it is untrue. The verbs are not interchangeable in every context.
usage: Transitive verb: reFUSE, with second-syllable stress and final /z/.

originalSense.definition: To decline (a request or demand).
originalSense.example: My request for a pay rise was refused.

distinctionTask.prompt: Reject an offer: _____ it. Say an allegation is untrue: deny it.
distinctionTask.explanation: Refuse and deny take different typical objects and meanings.

definition: To decline to act or give permission.
example: He refused to sign the incomplete form.
distinctions: Refuse normally takes a to-infinitive when an action is stated: refuse to sign. Avoid normally takes an -ing form; deny signing means say that one did not sign.
usage: Intransitive or followed by a to-infinitive; second-syllable stress.

originalSense.definition: To decline a request or demand, forbear; to withhold permission.
originalSense.example: I refuse to listen to this nonsense any more.

distinctionTask.prompt: The ordinary construction is “He refused _____ the form”.
distinctionTask.explanation: Refuse takes a to-infinitive for the declined action.

definition: To withhold something from someone or deny them access to it.
example: The office refused her permission to enter the archive.
distinctions: Refuse her permission gives the person an indirect object and the withheld thing a direct object. Refuse to enter instead means decline the action oneself.
usage: Ditransitive verb; second-syllable stress and final /z/.

originalSense.definition: To withhold (something) from (someone); to not give it to them or to bar them from having it.
originalSense.example: If we bang or scream they will spray us with some pepper or something else that's in an aeresol ^([sic]) can, and they wear gas masks, while the rest of us have to breathe the fumes in, and it makes us very sick and they refuse us medical treatment.

definition: To hold part of a military line back from its usual alignment.
example: In the military account, “refuse the right wing” means keep that wing back from the main alignment.
distinctions: This military refuse describes the position of part of a line; it is not a refusal to obey an order.
usage: Specialised military terminology. The note explains the source phrase without giving tactical instructions.

originalSense.definition: To throw back, or cause to keep back (as the centre, a wing, or a flank), out of the regular alignment when troops are about to engage the enemy.
originalSense.example: to refuse the right wing while the left wing attacks

definition: To disown or renounce someone or something.
example: In the older line “Refuse thy name”, refuse means renounce the name.
distinctions: This obsolete use concerns renouncing something; the common refusal verb can instead mean decline an offer or request.
usage: Obsolete. The reading note explains the recorded phrase.

originalSense.definition: To disown.
originalSense.example: Refuse thy name.

definition: A refusal or rejection.
example: In the older phrase “a proud refuse”, refuse is a noun meaning refusal.
distinctions: This obsolete noun names an act of refusing; the modern waste noun refuse names discarded material.
usage: Obsolete. Use refusal for this sense in ordinary modern writing.

originalSense.definition: refusal
originalSense.example: This ſpoken, readie with a proud refuſe [...]

definition: To fuse material again, as by heating or melting.
example: The glassworker refused the fragments into a single piece.
distinctions: This verb is re- plus fuse, meaning fuse again. The spelling re-fuse makes it clearer than refuse meaning decline.
usage: Materials-processing use, with a long re- vowel and main stress on fuse. The sentence is a vocabulary illustration, not a process specification.

originalSense.definition: To fuse again, as with, or after, heating or melting.

distinctionTask.prompt: In the materials sense, refuse or re-fuse means fuse _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The prefix re- means again; this is separate from refuse meaning decline.

definition: A romantic approach or expression of courtship.
example: In the older phrase “his Addresses to me”, addresses means his romantic approaches.
distinctions: These older addresses are approaches in courtship; a postal address identifies a delivery location.
usage: Archaic, chiefly plural. The note explains the recorded phrase.

originalSense.definition: A polite approach made to another person, especially of a romantic nature; an amorous advance.

definition: A manner or style of speaking or writing to someone.
example: In the phrase “a man of pleasing … address”, address refers to his manner of speaking to people.
distinctions: Manner of address concerns how someone speaks; an address meaning a speech is an instance of communication.
usage: Often older or formal. The note explains the source collocation.

originalSense.definition: A manner of speaking or writing to another; language, style.

definition: A formal appeal, petition or communication to a sovereign or head of state.
example: The assembly adopted an address to the head of state requesting a response.
distinctions: This address is a formal communication or appeal; a postal address gives delivery details. Its constitutional effect depends on the procedure.
usage: Diplomatic or political terminology.

originalSense.definition: A formal approach to a sovereign or head of state, especially an official appeal or petition.

definition: A formal response by a house of parliament to the sovereign’s opening speech.
example: The House debated the Address in Reply to the sovereign’s speech.
distinctions: The Address in Reply responds to the opening speech; it is not the speech delivered by the sovereign. Procedures and names vary across parliaments.
usage: Commonwealth parliamentary terminology.

originalSense.definition: A response given by each of the Houses of Parliament to the sovereign's speech at the opening of Parliament.

distinctionTask.prompt: The Address in Reply is a parliamentary _____ to the sovereign’s opening speech.
options: alternative name for the sovereign’s speech itself
distinctionTask.explanation: The response and the opening speech are different communications.

definition: A speech or formal communication to a person or audience, or its recorded text.
example: The principal gave a short address at the graduation ceremony.
distinctions: An address here is a speech; an address on an envelope identifies where correspondence should go.
usage: Noun. Second-syllable stress is usual in British English; noun stress can vary in North American English.

originalSense.definition: An act of addressing oneself to a person or group; a discourse or speech, or a record of this.

distinctionTask.prompt: The principal’s opening address was a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: An address to an audience is a speech or formal communication.

definition: The delivery details identifying a property or recipient’s location.
example: Please write the return address on the envelope.
distinctions: An address describes a location for delivery; it is not the physical place itself in this sense. Address formats differ by country.
usage: Noun. Unlike some noun–verb pairs, address does not require a stress change: British English commonly stresses the second syllable in both.

originalSense.definition: A description of the location of a property, usually with at least a street name and number, name of a town, and now also a postal code; such a description as superscribed for direction on an envelope or letter.

distinctionTask.prompt: Unlike a fixed noun–verb stress rule, British address commonly stresses the _____ syllable in both uses.
distinctionTask.explanation: British English commonly uses adDRESS for both noun and verb. Other accent and use variants are recorded.

definition: The physical location of a property.
example: The courier went to the address but found nobody there.
distinctions: Going to an address visits the place; writing an address records its delivery details.
usage: Noun; a location sense extending from the written description.

originalSense.definition: The location of a property.

definition: A numerical identifier for a location in a computer’s memory address space.
example: In this example, memory address 100 contains the value 42.
distinctions: An address identifies a location; the value is what is stored there. Virtual addresses and physical addresses are different concepts, related by the system’s mapping where applicable.
usage: Computing. The diagram is illustrative and does not prescribe an actual machine’s addressing scheme.

originalSense.definition: A number identifying a specific storage location in computer memory.

distinctionTask.prompt: If address 100 contains 42, the stored value is _____ and the address is 100.
distinctionTask.explanation: An address identifies the location; the value is the information stored there.

definition: An identifier used to locate a network endpoint, recipient or resource.
example: The form asks for an email address such as learner@example.org.
distinctions: An email address identifies a mailbox or recipient; an IP address identifies a network interface in context, and a URL identifies a resource. These are related kinds of address, not identical formats.
usage: Networking and Internet usage. example.org is reserved for examples.

originalSense.definition: A string of characters identifying a node or range of nodes on a network (especially the Internet), such as an e-mail address, IP address or URL.

definition: Readiness, skill or resourcefulness in handling a task.
example: In the older phrase “no small degree of address”, address means skill or resourcefulness.
distinctions: This rare address concerns skill in managing a situation; a mailing address concerns delivery details.
usage: Now rare. The note explains the source quotation that had been attached only to the broad Preparation heading.

originalSense.definition: Preparedness for some task; resourcefulness; skill, ability.

definition: The act of preparing or getting ready.
example: In the older line “she makes address to speak”, address means preparation to speak.
distinctions: This obsolete noun names the act of preparation; address meaning skill names a capability.
usage: Obsolete. The note explains Milton’s recorded wording.

originalSense.definition: The act of getting ready; preparation.

definition: The act or position of preparing the golf club and body to strike the ball.
example: The coach observed the golfer’s address of the ball before the swing.
distinctions: Address is preparation for a golf stroke, not the stroke itself. This is distinct from a spoken address.
usage: Golf; the source records Scottish usage. The example illustrates terminology rather than prescribing technique.

originalSense.definition: The act of bringing the head of the club up to the ball in preparation for swinging. <ref name=DSL></ref>

definition: Guidance or help.
usage: Obsolete; a distinct use example is still awaiting verification.

originalSense.definition: Guidance; help.

definition: A weighted plummet on a line, traditionally used to measure water depth.
example: The museum displays a sounding lead beside its line.
distinctions: A sounding lead is a weight used for depth measurements; a ship’s log measures speed. The source also records a related speed-estimation use.
usage: Nautical; pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: A plummet or mass of lead attached to a line, used in sounding depth at sea or to estimate velocity in knots.
originalSense.example: Although I could distinctly see the bottom, yet, heaving the lead, I found the ship in fifteen fathoms.

definition: A thin strip of type metal inserted between lines of metal type.
example: In historical printing, a lead is a physical strip separating lines of type.
distinctions: This lead is a physical strip; leading also names the resulting spacing.
usage: Historical printing; pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: A thin strip of type metal, used to separate lines of type in printing.

definition: Vertical spacing between lines of text, also called leading.
example: The designer increased the lead between the lines to improve readability.
distinctions: Lead here concerns vertical line spacing; tracking concerns spacing between characters. Modern interfaces usually call this leading or line spacing.
usage: Typography; pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: Vertical space in advance of a row or between rows of text. Also known as leading.
originalSense.example: This copy has too much lead; I prefer less space between the lines.

definition: Lead sheets or plates used as roof covering.
example: The contractor replaced the damaged roof lead.
distinctions: Roof lead names the covering material; a lead meaning a covered roof names the roof as a whole.
usage: Roofing; pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: Sheets or plates of lead used as a covering for roofs.

definition: A roof covered with lead sheets or terne plates.
example: In older building descriptions, the leads can mean the lead-covered roof.
distinctions: This countable roof sense differs from uncountable lead meaning the metal or roofing material.
usage: Often older and plural; pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: A roof covered with lead sheets or terne plates.
originalSense.example: I would have the tower two stories, and goodly leads upon the top.

definition: The thin writing core of a pencil, usually made from graphite.
example: The lead in my mechanical pencil broke.
distinctions: Pencil lead is graphite-based; the name does not mean that ordinary pencil cores contain elemental lead.
usage: Pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: A thin cylinder of graphite used in pencils.

distinctionTask.prompt: The writing core called pencil lead is usually made from _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Ordinary pencil lead is graphite-based.

definition: Bullets or ammunition, in slang.
example: In a crime novel, lead may be slang for bullets or ammunition.
distinctions: The slang names ammunition, while the ordinary material sense names the metal.
usage: Slang; reading recognition; pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: Bullets; ammunition.
originalSense.example: They pumped him full of lead.

definition: Lead-lined protective clothing used in X-ray work.
example: The technician checked the leads for damage before use.
distinctions: Plural leads can mean protective garments; a lead can also be an electrical wire. The protective context determines the reading.
usage: Medical workplace terminology, plural; pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: X-ray protective clothing lined with lead.
originalSense.example: You must remember to wear your leads.

definition: To cover, fill or otherwise treat something with lead.
example: The restorer leaded the glass panels using narrow strips of the metal.
distinctions: This material verb is lead–leaded–leaded; the guide verb is lead–led–led. “Led” in this example would be the wrong past form.
usage: Material verb; pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: To cover, fill, or affect with lead.
originalSense.example: continuous firing leads the grooves of a rifle.

definition: To insert metal spacing strips between lines of type.
example: In historical printing, to lead type is to add strips between its lines.
distinctions: The printing verb has past tense leaded; the guide verb has past tense led.
usage: Historical printing; pronounced /led/.

originalSense.definition: To place leads between the lines of.
originalSense.example: to lead a page

definition: Source grouping: guiding, directing and influencing.

originalSense.definition: To guide or conduct.

distinctions: Lead can be intransitive, with no direct object; lead the group states the object explicitly.
usage: Verb /liːd/; past tense and past participle led /led/.

originalSense.definition: To guide or conduct, as by accompanying, going before, showing, influencing, directing with authority, etc.; to have precedence or preeminence; to be first or chief; — used in most of the senses of the transitive verb.

lead someone up the garden path

example: The narrow path leads to the station.

originalSense.definition: To tend or reach in a certain spatial direction, or to a certain place.
originalSense.example: the path leads to the mill

lead someone up the garden path

definition: To cause or contribute to a result, usually with to.
example: Poor ventilation can lead to condensation.

definition: To live or experience a particular kind of life.
example: After retiring, she led an active life.
distinctions: Lead a life describes how someone lives; lead a group describes guiding or managing people.

originalSense.definition: To live or experience (a particular way of life).

definition: A correspondence, equivalent or counterpart.
example: The search found an exact match for the sample code.
distinctions: An exact match agrees on the compared features; a rough match is only approximate. The comparison criterion must be clear.
usage: Noun /mætʃ/.

originalSense.definition: Equivalence; a state of correspondence; a counterpart.

definition: An agreement or compact, in an older recorded use.
example: In the recorded agreement sense, match can mean an agreement or compact.
distinctions: This recorded agreement use should not be confused with a sports contest or treated as the ordinary modern word for every contract.
usage: Older or uncommon use; reading recognition.

originalSense.definition: An agreement or compact.

definition: A marriage or marital union.
example: Their families described the marriage as a happy match.
distinctions: A match can name the marriage; it can also name a person considered as a possible spouse. Suitability is a separate judgment.
usage: Marriage usage; noun /mætʃ/.

originalSense.definition: A marriage.

definition: A person considered as a potential spouse.
example: In the novel, the family regarded him as a suitable match.
distinctions: This match is a person considered for marriage, rather than the marriage itself. The expression reflects the speaker’s perspective.
usage: Often traditional or historical social usage; noun /mætʃ/.

originalSense.definition: A candidate for matrimony; one to be gained in marriage.
